Immunofluorescence analysis of ANXA1 and SNAIL1 confirmed the state distinctions: TGFβ1 alone induced SNAIL1 expression, whereas YAP activation increased ANXA1, but these states remained overlapping under single-treatment conditions. Only combined treatment produced spatially separated ANXA1high and SNAIL1high populations as quantified by signal anticorrelation (Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 12c), recapitulating the in vivo patient distribution (Fig. 3c,d). YAP activation also triggered nuclear shape changes and loss of heterochromatin (Extended Data Fig. 12d–f). Consistently, reanalysis of the patient tumour spatial transcriptomic data confirmed that fragmented architectures highlighted reduced enrichment of heterochromatin regulators (Extended Data Fig. 12g,h). This was validated at the protein level by H3K9me2,3 immunostaining of patient samples (Extended Data Fig. 12i,j). Loss of heterochromatin was associated with increased nuclear circularity (Extended Data Fig. 12k), providing a mechanistic link between YAP signalling, nuclear shape and tissue architecture.

In a recent development, to determine whether these cell-state transitions were coupled to behavioural consequences, we analysed organoid dynamics. Untreated organoids displayed spheroid morphology with expansive low-level growth. TGFβ1 induced cohesive invasion without substantially enhancing overall net invasion, while YAP activation triggered dispersive invasion. Combined treatment further increased the prevalence of dispersive invasion (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Video 1).

To assess the in vivo relevance of these behavioural changes, patient-derived organoids (line 2) treated with LATS inhibitor, TGFβ1 or both were orthotopically transplanted into the mouse colon by endoscopy50 (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12l). Untreated organoids did not generate visible tumours, whereas all three treatment conditions did so with variable efficiency. Mice receiving combined YAP activation and TGFβ1 treatment generated tumours (Fig. 5h,i) and, as expected, YAP activation enhanced nuclear YAP in the transplanted tumours while TGFβ1 treatment enhanced SMAD2/3 activation (Extended Data Fig. 12m). Quantitative analysis revealed that the combination treatment produced the largest tumours and the only tumours that invaded the stroma (Fig. 5i). Consistently, ANXA1 expression was elevated in YAP-activated transplants but was highest in combination-treated tumours (Extended Data Fig. 12n), collectively demonstrating that cell state diversification drives tumour aggressiveness in vivo.

Recent findings suggest that together, these experiments demonstrate that tissue architecture and stromal signals collaborate to drive cell-state diversification and invasive behaviour. Architectural confinement suppresses β-catenin signalling to promote regenerative SC identity, while soluble stromal signals enhance EMT features. The combination of mechanical, compositional and signalling inputs from the microenvironment drives diversification into distinct SC and EMT states and potentiates tumour invasion.

Recent findings suggest that identifying the mechanisms that drive intratumoural heterogeneity is central to improving diagnostic precision and treatment outcomes in CRC. We demonstrate that tumour architecture and associated nuclear morphology are strong independent prognostic indicators, and that these features co-evolve with cell states within individual tumours. Fragmented architectures specifically associate with transition from LGR5-marked adult SCs to a fetal-like/regenerative state linked to aggressive behaviour and poor prognosis8.

According to recent reports, the prognostic power of architecture derives from its co-evolution with plastic, aggressive cell states. Chemotherapy, wounding, inflammation and mechanical damage are known to reactivate fetal and regenerative SC programmes in CRC34,51,52,53,54,55. TGFβ1 drives WNT independence and fetal-like lineage conversion in CRC organoids56, and fibrotic stromal stiffening promotes aggression across solid tumours57. Our data implicate compressive forces from stiffened ECM in distorting tissue geometry, inducing fragmentation and promoting adult-to-regenerative SC transition. The regenerative state emerges as a hybrid with EMT features that TGFβ1 and stromal signals further diversify into spatially proximal but transcriptionally distinct SC and EMT states, suggesting a continuum in which the balance of signals determines which state predominates. Coupling of this diversification to invasion explains the association between fragmented architecture and poor prognosis, supporting a model in which disrupted tissue organization and inflammatory signalling initiate a feedforward loop driving disease aggression.

Our image analysis framework, combining nuclear and epithelial membrane immunostaining with machine-learning-based classification, offers an efficient stratification strategy independent of mutational status, and suggests that quantitative architectural analysis could serve as a tractable proxy for tumour heterogeneity in clinical decision-making.

The study uses a previously described cohort58 comprising 1,342 patients who underwent resection for colorectal cancer at Central Finland Central Hospital between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2015 and had adequate tumour samples available. Formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour samples were obtained from the pathology archives of the Central Finland Central Hospital Nova, which covers all colorectal cancers diagnosed in Central Finland (the population of the area averaged around 270,000 during the study period). Associated clinical data were collected from clinical patient records by study physicians. Moreover, all tumours were previously re-evaluated for disease stage, tumour grade (WHO 2019 criteria), mismatch repair (MMR) status, BRAF V600E mutation status and the presence of lymphovascular invasion58. Analyses of this cohort were approved by the Regional medical research ethics committee of the Wellbeing services county of Central Finland (Dnro 13U/2011, 1/2016, 8/2020 and 2/2023) andthe Finnish Medicines Agency (Fimea, FIMEA/2023/001573). The need to obtain informed consent from the study patients was waived (Dnro FIMEA/2023/001573).

Recent findings suggest that the validation dataset was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee at Helsinki University Hospital (HUS/1223/2021). Permission to use archive samples without informed consent was granted by the Finnish National Supervisory Authority of Health and Welfare (permit number Valvira Dnro 1004/06.01.03.01/2012) and the FIMEA Finnish Medicines Agency (permit number FIMEA Dnro 2021/006901). Final TMA blocks of duplicate 1.2 mm cores were made in TMA Grand Master (3D Histech). For spatial transcriptomics selected full tumour samples from the same cohort were used. The authors affirm that the study was conducted following the rules of the Declaration of Helsinki of 1975, revised in 2013.

Collagen analyses were performed on a previously described cohort59 comprising an independent cohort of 1,011 patients who underwent resection for stage I–IV CRC at Oulu University Hospital between 2006 and 2020. The analysis was based on TMAs that included four 1.2-mm-diameter cores, two from the IM and two from the CT. Analyses of this cohort were approved by the Regional medical research ethics committee of the Wellbeing services county of North Ostrobothnia (37/2020). The patients gave written informed consent for the study. Final TMA blocks of duplicate 1.2 mm IM and CT cores were made in TMA Grand Master (TMA Master II). For this cohort all tumours were previously re-evaluated for disease stage, tumour grade (WHO 2019 criteria), MMR status, BRAF V600E mutation status, tumour budding based on the International Tumor Budding Consensus Conference (ITBCC) criteria30, and the presence of lymphovascular invasion58. CD3+ and CD8+ T cell densities were quantified separately in the CT and IM, converted into percentile values, averaged across the four resulting measures and categorized as low (0–25), intermediate (>25–70) or high (>70–100), following the main principles of the Immunoscore assay.

Recent findings suggest that immunofluorescence staining and imaging of TMAs was performed as previously described60 for pan-cadherin antibodies to label the tumour cells and their plasma membranes and the nuclear marker DAPI. Imaging was performed using the Zeiss Axio Scan.Z1 slide scanner, with each round of staining recorded as an independent image. The CZI image file contained up to five fluorescent channels. For the full tumour samples, the staining was carried out on the same slides as spatial transcriptomics, after the spatial transcriptomics analyses. To select ROIs for sample collection for transcriptome analysis, the slides were stained with Syto13, pan-CK (AF532), CD45 (AF594) and αSMA (AF647)A to visualize nuclei, epithelial cells, immune cells and stroma, respectively. Imaging of the staining was performed on the DSP instrument using 50, 200, 200, 200 ms on the FITC, CY3, Texas Red and CY5 channels, respectively. After quenching the signal, the slides were restained for the indicated markers and the signal was imaged on the DSP instrument. The single-channel images were loaded to HALO v.3.6 image analysis software for visualization, registered based on the nuclear signal and fused to generate a composite image with 8 markers (including the nuclei).

Multiplexed fluorescence immunohistochemical staining and imaging was performed in 4–6 cycles as previously described60 for two sets of antibodies, listed below, and the nuclear marker DAPI. After the first-round staining and whole-slide imaging, the fluorescence signal was bleached, the antibodies from the first-round staining were denatured and subsequent staining rounds were performed. Imaging was performed on the Zeiss Axio Scan.Z1 slide scanner with each round of staining saved as a separate .CZI image file.

The following primary antibodies were used: αSMA (Dako, M0851; 1:500, 1 h at room temperature), β-catenin (Cell Marque, 224M-14; 1:500, 1.5 h at room temperature), E-cadherin (BD Biosciences, 610182; 1:200, 1 h at room temperature), CDX2 (Cell Signaling, 23083; 1:1,000, 1 h at room temperature), H3K9me2/3 (Cell Signaling, 5327; 1:200, 1 h at room temperature), pan-cytokeratin (Abcam, ab7753; 1:150, 1 h at room temperature), pan-cytokeratin (Invitrogen, MA5-13156; 1:100, 1 h at room temperature), PROX1 (Cell Signaling, 45546; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), Ki-67 (Dako, M7240; 1:100, 1 h at room temperature), tenascin C (R&D Systems, MAB2138; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), vimentin (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-6260; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486; 1:500, overnight at 4 °C), YAP1 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-101199; 1:50, overnight at 4 °C) and a collagen-binding peptide (generated by the laboratory of V. Weaver61; 1:500, overnight at 4 °C). For pan-epithelial (pan-EPI) cocktail staining, the antibodies (Abcam, ab7753; Invitrogen, MA5-13156; and BD Biosciences, 610182) were combined, each at 1:200, and applied for 2 h at room temperature.

Immunofluorescence staining and imaging of TMAs was performed as previously described60 for pan-cadherin antibodies to label the tumour cells and their plasma membranes and the nuclear marker DAPI.

Sources indicate that preprocessing and segmentation were performed essentially as described previously36. In brief, TMA cores were de-arrayed using built-in tools from QuPath (v.0.5.1)62. Cores exhibiting folding artifacts, blurriness or limited tumour content were excluded from analysis. After preprocessing, nuclei were segmented based on DAPI signal using custom-trained Cellpose 2.0 models (v.2.0 and v.2.2.2)63, separately optimized for the TMA and whole-slide image datasets. The tumour and stromal compartments were identified using a multi-label U-Net trained on 30 representative cores. Pixel-level annotations were generated manually in ilastik (v.1.4.0)64 based on pan-EPI staining.

Tumour architectural subtypes were classified through a transfer-learning pipeline comprising four stages:.

Stage 1, tiling: each TMA core image was subdivided into non-overlapping 448 × 448 px (208 × 208 µm) tiles covering the full tissue area.

According to recent reports, stage 2, feature embedding: a multi-label U-Net was trained to segment architectural subtypes. Ground-truth masks were derived from the tumour–stroma segmentations described above, with tumour regions manually re-annotated according to three architectural subtypes: glandular (organized, lumen-forming structures), fragmented (disrupted tumour clusters) and solid (dense). Two additional classes (stroma and edge/background) were included to handle non-tumour regions. The training set comprised 196 cores selected as unambiguous archetypes of each architectural subtype. The validity of this selection was assessed by computing silhouette scores on a panel of interpretable morphological features (Fig. 1f) and comparing the archetype score to a null distribution generated from 1,000 size-matched random draws of cohort cores assigned matching per-class labels (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Each tile was then passed through the trained U-Net, and the activations at the deepest convolutional layer (bottleneck) were aggregated through global average pooling to yield a compact feature vector per tile, encoding the dominant morphological pattern without requiring a separate hand-crafted feature design.

Stage 3, tile-level classification: a multinomial logistic regression classifier (L-BFGS solver, scikit-learn) was trained on the bottleneck embeddings to assign each tile to one of five classes: glandular, fragmented, solid, stroma or edge/background. Features were standardized before classification. The training set comprised 1,154 manually annotated tiles (365 glandular, 251 fragmented, 148 solid, 199 stroma and 191 edge/background), randomly sampled from 760 cores across the cohort. Performance was evaluated using stratified fivefold cross-validation. At inference, the classifier output five class probabilities per tile; tiles dominated by edge or stroma (probability ≥ 0.5) were excluded, and the remaining glandular, fragmented and solid probabilities were renormalized to sum to one before assigning each tile to its most probable architectural subtype (argmax).

Sources indicate that stage 4, patient-level classification: tile-level predictions were aggregated per sample. The proportion of tumour-classified tiles belonging to each architectural subtype was computed separately for the CT (centre of the tumour) and IM. If a single subtype accounted for more than 50% of tiles, the sample was classified as that dominant architecture; otherwise, it was labelled mixed. The trained U-Net can be reused to extract morphological embeddings from other colorectal cancer datasets, provided that a membrane staining is available and that tissue tiles are of comparable physical size to those used in this study (448 × 448 pixels, corresponding to approximately 208 × 208 µm at the imaging resolution used here); tiles acquired at a different pixel resolution can be resampled (downsampled or upsampled) to match the model’s input size. However, the tile-level logistic regression classifier generally requires retraining to account for dataset-specific differences such as staining variability, imaging conditions or cohort composition. This is the strategy that we followed when applying the pipeline to the validation and multiplex datasets in this study: the U-Net embeddings were extracted directly, while the classifier was retrained on a new set of annotated tiles for each dataset. For the validation dataset, the classifier was retrained by supplementing the original training set with 205 additional annotated tiles (44 glandular, 49 fragmented, 28 solid, 50 stroma and 34 edge/background). For the multiplex dataset, 1,886 tiles were independently annotated (740 glandular, 446 fragmented, 123 solid, 491 stroma and 86 edge/background) and used to train a separate classifier. The pretrained U-Net model is available in ONNX format at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20343193).

Sources indicate that branch lengths were quantified from the binary tumour mask by first removing small objects (<20 px) and filling small holes (<100 px area), then skeletonizing the mask using skimage.morphology.skeletonize. Small spurious branches with an arc length of shorter than 5 pixels were removed by pruning using the skan library. Branch lengths were measured as geodesic arc lengths along the skeleton paths (√2-weighted pixel distances) using skan.summarize()[‘branch-distance’].

The global contour roughness of the tumour boundary was assessed by extracting all contours from the binary tumour mask at level 0.5 using skimage.measure.find_contours. Contours with fewer than five points were discarded. The remaining contours were smoothed with a Gaussian filter (σ = 1) to reduce pixel noise. Pointwise curvature κ for a smoothed contour (x(s), y(s)) was computed by finite differences:.

Industry observers note that where primes denote derivatives with respect to the contour parameter. Absolute curvature values were summed over all contours and normalized by the total number of contour points N to yield mean roughness per unit length.

Sources indicate that lumens within the binary tumour mask were detected by filling all holes (scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes) and subtracting the original mask. The resulting lumen mask was labelled, and each lumen area (in pixels) was measured through skimage.measure.regionprops.

In a recent development, for each cell centroid, the Euclidean distances to its k = 3 nearest neighbours were computed using sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors with a BallTree algorithm. For each cell, the mean, s.d., coefficient of variation and maximum of the k neighbour distances were stored as features.

Recent findings suggest that the local nuclear orientation order (Ψk) was computed for each cell using its k = 3 nearest neighbours. For each neighbour, the orientation angle θ was obtained by projecting the cell’s orientation vector (defined by its longest axis) onto a fixed reference direction. The nematic order parameter was then calculated as:.

yielding a value between 0 (random orientations) and 1 (perfectly aligned neighbours).

Stroma proximity was determined by computing, for each tumour cell centroid, the minimum Euclidean distance to the set of stroma cell centroids using pairwise distance computation (scipy.spatial.distance.cdist).

Tumour–stroma ratio was calculated by measuring the total pixel areas of the tumour and stroma compartments from the segmentation mask and computing the ratio of tumour pixel count to stroma pixel count.

The fragmentation index was computed by first constructing a spatial proximity graph of all tumour cell centroids, where an edge connects any two cells of which the Euclidean distance is within 80 pixels (radius-based connectivity using a BallTree). Louvain community detection was then applied to this unweighted graph to partition cells into spatially coherent communities. The fragmentation index was calculated as the number of detected communities divided by the cell count.

Whole-core fluorescence images were segmented into 12 tissue compartments with a multi-scale tumour/stroma classifier, and tumour islands were defined as connected components of the tumour class on the cleaned compartment map after upsampling to image resolution. The stromal compartment was restricted to a strict definition that excluded muscle, vessel, adipose, dense-stroma and debris classes. For each tumour island, a peri-tumoural region of interest was constructed as the 50 µm band immediately outside the island border, intersected with the strict stroma mask. Within this region, fibre body masks were obtained for the collagen I and TNC channels (analysed independently) using a fine-tuned U-Net applied at a probability threshold of 0.5.

From each body mask, we derived three independent descriptors of the underlying fibre network65: (1) the box-counting fractal dimension of the binarized mask, capturing network roughness and branching complexity; (2) the mean structure-tensor coherence within the mask, ranging from 0 for isotropic networks to 1 for perfectly aligned fibres; and (3) the median local fibre thickness, computed as twice the Euclidean distance transform sampled along the fibre skeleton and converted to micrometres using a pixel size of 0.325 µm. Features were emitted per (image × island × channel × distance band × stroma definition × architecture) so that all downstream summaries remained traceable to the underlying islands and fluorescence pixels. To avoid within-image pseudoreplication, every subsequent comparison was performed on per-(image × architecture) means, obtained by averaging each feature across the islands sharing the same architecture within an image.

Whole-slide image immunostainings were registered using the warpy workflow in ImageJ and QuPath. Whole-slide images were subsequently divided into non-overlapping tiles of 1,000 × 1,000 pixels and selected for downstream analysis in a manner analogous to TMAs, including tumour/stroma classification and nuclear segmentation. For each nucleus, the average nuclear intensity of markers (ANXA1, SNAIL1) was quantified. For cytoplasmic markers (E-cadherin, ANXA1, VIM), the nuclear contour was dilated by 5 pixels to approximate the cytoplasmic region, from which the average cytoplasmic intensity was computed. Single-cell profiles were then clustered using the Leiden algorithm at a resolution of 0.1.

Sources indicate that for each whole-slide-image tile, we computed a spatial-coherence score that quantifies whether cells with the same label group together or segregate. First, for every cell we counted its 12 immediate closest neighbours that shared the same label and averaged this count across all cells in the tile. Next, we generated a null range by randomly shuffling the position of all cells 100 times, repeating the same neighbour counting for each shuffle; the average value from these shuffled sets was taken as the expected mean. The score was then calculated as (observed – expected_mean)/(expected_max – expected_mean). A score above zero means cells with the same label cluster together more than would be expected by chance (attraction), a value of zero corresponds to a random arrangement and a negative value denotes spatial repulsion, where same-label cells are less likely to be adjacent than expected by chance.

According to recent reports, TMA cores were identified using the dearrayer functionality in QuPath. Background illumination correction and background subtraction were subsequently performed for each core and staining round using PyBaSiC. TMAs were registered across six staining rounds using the DAPI channel as a reference. All cores underwent semi-manual quality control to remove samples that were damaged, exhibited poor registration or contained absent/very low tumour content.

Recent findings suggest that nuclear segmentation was performed using the Cellpose cyto3 model with the DAPI channel as the input. Tissue pixels were classified into tumour, stroma, tissue fold, autofluorescence, necrosis and background using an iterative supervised approach in ilastik until good visual agreement between pan-EPI signal and tumour masks was achieved across cores. For each cell, mean marker intensities were extracted using pyradiomics, and nuclear shape features were computed using a custom Python pipeline. To approximate cytoplasmic signal, nuclear masks were expanded by three pixels using expand_labels from skimage. We also computed, for each nucleus, the mean value of the ilastik pixel-classification probability map to derive cell-level classification confidence metrics.

In a recent development, before clustering, cells with extreme nuclear areas were removed by excluding the lowest 1st percentile and highest 99th percentile. Tumour cells were then selected based on a tumour probability threshold of >0.5 and processed using a standard Scanpy workflow. Data were scaled using scanpy.pp.scale with max_value = 10, such that values were truncated to a maximum of 10 after scaling. Principal component analysis was performed using the maximum available number of components, and a k-nearest-neighbour graph was constructed with n_neighbors = 50. Clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm with the igraph-based implementation.

For patient-level grouping, normalized phenotype distributions were used as input for hierarchical clustering (Ward linkage). The number of patient groups was determined based on biological interpretability and stability of the resulting clusters.

Tile-level U-Net embeddings were z-scored and used to build a k-nearest-neighbour graph, visualized by t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE). Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) was computed on the three architecture classes (glandular, fragmented, solid, assigned by argmax of the renormalized U-Net probabilities after removing edge and stroma tiles) and overlaid on the t-SNE. Diffusion pseudotime was computed from a diffusion map of the same embeddings, rooted at the most confident glandular tile, and tiles were grouped into 40 equal-width pseudotime bins. Within each bin, architecture probabilities were averaged, and cell phenotype fractions (cells assigned to tiles by centroid position) were averaged and renormalized to unit sum.

Spatial transcriptomics was performed using the GeoMX-DSP platform (Nanostring/Bruker). Eight patients with stage II/III CRC were selected from the TMA cohort based on presence of architecturally heterogeneous tumours. Samples were prepared according to recommendations from the vendor for FFPE slides, including baking for 60 min at 60 °C, dewaxing and antigen retrieval with ER2 for 20 min at 100 °C, fixation in NBF (10%), incubation in NBF stop and proteinase K treatment (15 min at 37 °C). These steps were performed on the Leica BondRX autostainer. The slides were incubated with the probes overnight and, after stringent washes, were stained with Syto13, pan-cytokeratin (AF532), αSMA (custom conjugated on AF647) and CD45 (AF594) antibodies to detect tumour and stromal microenvironments. ROIs (67, 61, 96 and 59 for the four slides, carrying patients 1 and 2, 3 and 5, 4 and 6, and 7 and 8, respectively) were segmented for pan-cytokeratin positivity to collect 82, 94, 141 and 63 areas of interest (AOIs) representing tumour and tumour–stroma boundary. Each ROI yielded a tumour AOI and, where collected, a stroma AOI. Transcriptomic analyses of the tumour compartment (Figs. 2f, 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 10a) used the 249 tumour AOIs from 8 patients. After scanning, tissue sections were additionally stained with antibodies against SNAIL1 (Santa Cruz, sc-271977), E-cadherin (BD, 610182), ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486) and VIM (Santa Cruz, sc-6260) and imaged using Phenoimager (Akoya Biosciences).

Quality control of the sequencing data was performed in R using GeoMx packages, following standard GeoMx QC guidelines. Segment filtering employed the following thresholds: minimum reads per segment (AOI) = 1,000, minimum percentage of reads trimmed = 80, minimum percentage of reads stitched = 80, minimum percentage of reads aligned = 75, minimum sequencing saturation = 50, minimum negative control counts = 1, maximum counts in the NTC (no-template control) well = 9,000.

Sources indicate that segments with low signal were removed based on the limit of quantification. Gene filtering was applied by both compartment (tumour/stroma) and architecture type to preserve important genes in underrepresented regions. A 10% segment cut-off was used. Data were normalized using the third quartile (Q3) method.

For differential gene expression, raw counts were analysed using the PyDESeq2 Python package, with patient sample included as a covariate to control for interpatient variability. For each gene, a Wald test was used to assess differential expression; multiple-testing correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the FDR. Genes with an adjusted P value (q value) below 0.05 were considered significantly differentially expressed.

Sources indicate that gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the prerank function from the GSEApy Python package with 1,000 permutations. Before analysis, all genes were ranked according to their effect sizes (log-transformed fold changes) derived from the differential expression analysis. The following gene sets from previous studies were included. EMT gene sets: Wound response GO GP66, mesenchymal67, matrix remodelling68, TGFB activation (TGFB KEGG, TGFB CORE GENES/TGFB1/TGFB2)68,69, EMT activation (EMT Core Genes)67, EMT Hallmark70, pEMT71, EMT-II (MP13)72. SC gene sets: crypt base32, LGR5 intestinal SCs33, fetal8, regenerative34 and revival colonic SCs52. High-relapse gene sets: epithelial-specific high-risk gene set, core high-relapse cells73.

According to recent reports, trajectory analysis was performed using PAGA74 with the sc.tl.paga function built into Scanpy (v.1.9.6)75. To prepare the data, we first selected 3,000 highly variable genes using the seurat flavour of sc.pp.highly_variable_genes. Next, we calculated and selected 100 principal components (PCs) using sc.tl.pca. PCs were batch-corrected using Harmony (v.0.0.9)76 to correct for patient-specific gene expression profiles. Finally, nearest neighbours were calculated using sc.pp.neighbors (n_neighbors = 30) on the corrected PCs and PAGA was run on tumour architecture types.

We calculated diffusion pseudotime (DPT77) using the sc.tl.diffmap and sc.tl.dpt functions from Scanpy (v.1.9.6)75. In preparation, for a patient sample, we selected 3,000 highly variable genes using the seurat flavour of sc.pp.highly_variable_genes. Next, we calculated 100 principal components (PCs) using sc.tl.pca. Finally, nearest neighbours were calculated using sc.pp.neighbors (n_neighbors = 30) on the corrected PCs. DPT was run using a cell in the glandular region of the tumour as a ‘root cell’, representing its most unperturbed region.

Industry observers note that the use of human CRC organoid cultures was approved as part of the iCAN Precision Medicine Flagship study reviewed by the HUS Ethical Committee and is executed based on a HUS research permit (4.5.2023 §38 (HUS/223/2023)), a Findata data permit (THL/1338/14.02.00/2022) and material transfer agreements with Helsinki Biobank (HBP20210170) and Finnish Hematology and Registry Biobank FHRB (12.5.2022). The underlying PANORG study collecting the samples to the iCAN Flagship was approved by the ethical committee of the Helsinki and Uusimaa hospital district and study site institutional review boards (PANORG ethical approval HUS/390/2021, HUS approval HUS/69/2022). The study participants provided written, informed consent for the protocols. Organoids were maintained in a mixture of 60% LWRN medium (originally established in ref. 78) and 40% human basal medium supplemented with rhEGF (R&D, 236-EG, 100 ng ml−1); LWRN was replaced with Advanced DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for no-WNT conditions. Organoids were subjected to single-cell sequencing and selected to harbour APC and TP53 mutations for the studies here.

Patient-derived CRC organoids were cultured in Matrigel or collagen (drug treatment experiment), after which single-cell suspensions were generated by incubation with cell recovery solution (30 min at 4 °C; Corning) followed by digestion with TrypLE Express Enzyme (5 min at 37 °C; Invitrogen). After washing with ice-cold DMEM, single cells were counted using Luna-II automated cell counter (Logos Biosystems) and loaded on a microwell cartridge of the BD Rhapsody Express system (BD) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Single-cell whole-transcriptome analysis libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions using the BD Rhapsody WTA Reagent kit (BD, 633802) and sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 500 system using the High Output Kit v2.5 (150 cycles, Illumina) for 2 × 75 bp paired-end reads with 8 bp single index aiming sequencing depth of >20,000 reads per cell for each sample.

Industry observers note that UMI, complex barcode, and sample tags were extracted from raw reads and demultiplexed using a custom script (rhapsody-demultiplex; https://github.com/Bioinformatics-Service-MPI-Munster/scrna-tools). Reads were mapped using STAR (v.2.7.10a)79 (--soloType CB_UMI_Complex --soloCellFilter None --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --soloFeatures GeneFull_Ex50pAS --soloAdapterSequence NNNNNNNNNGTGANNNNNNNNNGACA --soloCBmatchWLtype 1MM --soloCBposition 2_0_2_8 2_13_2_21 3_1_3_9 --soloUMIposition 3_10_3_17 --soloCBwhitelist BD_CLS1_v2_draft.txt BD_CLS2_v2_draft.txt BD_CLS3_v2_draft.txt --runRNGseed 1 --soloMultiMappers EM --readFilesCommand zcat --outSAMattributes NH HI AS nM NM MD jM jI MC ch CB UB GX GN). Raw counts were imported as AnnData (v.0.10.7)80 objects in Python (v.3.9.11). We removed low-complexity barcodes using the knee plot method (1,500–3,000 counts per cell) and further filtered out cells with a high mitochondrial mRNA percentage (>50%). Doublets were predicted with scrublet (v.0.2.3)81. Finally, each sample’s gene expression matrix was normalized using scran (v.1.26.2)82, with Leiden clustering83 input at resolution 0.5.

At this stage, the samples were merged with scanpy (v.1.10.1)75. For 2D embedding, expression values were cell cycle regressed using sc.tl.score_genes_cell_cycle with G2M and S-phase gene lists from ref. 84 and sc.pp.regress_out. The expression matrix was subset to the 3,000 most highly variable genes (sc.pp.highly_variable_genes, flavor=“seurat”). We calculated and selected the top 100 PCs (sc.tl.pca), which served as basis for k-nearest neighbour calculation (sc.pp.neighbors, n_neighbors = 30). Nearest neighbours were then used as an input for UMAP layout (sc.tl.umap, min_dist = 0.3). Leiden clusters were calculated using sc.tl.leiden at resolution 0.7. Pseudotime and gene set enrichment analyses were performed as described for the spatial transcriptomics datasets. For reanalysis of the published tumour in vivo data, we chose a cell in the most stem-like cluster according to CytoTRACE analysis.

For generation of consensus gene sets, EMT gene sets (mesenchymal67, matrix remodelling68, TGFB activation (TGFB KEGG, TGFB CORE GENES/TGFB1/TGFB2)68,69, EMT activation (EMT Core Genes67, EMT Hallmark70, pEMT71, EMT-II (MP13)72) and SC gene sets (crypt base32, LGR5 intestinal SCs33, fetal8, regenerative34 and revival colonic SCs52) were merged and overlapping genes within and across gene sets were removed to generate the Core-EMT, Core-CBC and Core-RegSC gene sets.

Sources indicate that all cells in the dataset were scored for the Core-EMT, Core-CBC and Core-RegSC gene sets using the Scanpy sc.tl.score_genes function. The scores were then converted to a per-dataset rank rescaled to [0, 1]. Cells were then ordered across the CBC to RegSC–EMT axis as a composite_trajectory = (RegSC_rank01 + EMT_rank01 − CBC_rank01 + 1)/3. Cells with composite_trajectory in the top 30% of the per-dataset distribution were classified hybrid.

For distribution across the EMT–RegSC axis, two curated marker panels were scored per hybrid cell with sc.tl.score_genes (random_state = 0): a RegSC-pole panel (GPRC5A, TSPAN1, PDZK1IP1, ANXA1, ANXA3, S100A6, S100A11, LCN2, SAA1, SAA2, KRT16, KRT17, SPP1, CD44, EMP1 and TACSTD2) and an EMT pole panel (SNAI1, SNAI2, ZEB1, ZEB2, TWIST1, TWIST2, VIM, FN1, S100A4, ACTA2, MMP14, PLAU, PLAUR, SERPINE1, TIMP1). Each panel score was z-scored within its dataset, and the pole axis was defined as axis_pole = z(score_EMT_pole) − z(score_RegSC_pole). The pole-axis shift among hybrid cells was computed as Cliff’s δ = 2 × U/(n_c × n_Unt) − 1, where U is the Mann–Whitney U statistic of axis pole over the two hybrid groups. δ ∈ [−1, +1]; δ < 0 represents that hybrid cells of c are shifted toward the regenerative pole relative to untreated-hybrid cells, δ > 0 represents that hybrid cells of c are shifted toward the EMT pole. By default, untreated sits at δ = 0.

In a recent development, hydrogel scaffolds were engineered as described previously42,85. A PDMS stamp (see below) with a crypt-mimicking array of pillar topography was placed in the central top reservoir of the chip. To generate the ECM for the chip, bovine TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50mL, Advanced Biomatrix) was neutralized according to the manufacturer’s instructions and then mixed with Matrigel (356231, Corning) at a 75/25 (v/v) ratio. After gel injection through gel-loading port, hydrogel was polymerized at 37 °C, 5% CO2 (hereafter referred to as incubator) for 15 min. After ECM polymerization, all chip reservoirs were topped up with PBS or cell culture medium.

In a recent development, stamps featuring crypt-mimicking microtopography were fabricated from PDMS by replica moulding of 2PP-printed models. First, arrays of colon crypt-mimicking micropillars were designed in Autodesk Fusion. Several topographies were tested and optimized, the final microtopography design consists of the slightly conical pillars, ranging from 50 to 120 µm in diameter (top to bottom) and 700 µm in height. The 3D model was printed using a NanoOne (UpNano) 2PP printer on glass coverslips with UpPhoto resin and a ×10/0.4 NA objective. To generate a master mould with inverted topography, the printed structures were plasma-activated and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning; 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio) was poured over the master, degassed under vacuum, and cured at 80 °C for 12 h. The resulting PDMS replica was cut, plasma-activated and silanized overnight as above. This PDMS negative was then used repeatedly as a mould for casting final PDMS stamps using the same procedure (Sylgard 184, 10:1 ratio, cured at 80 °C for 12 h).

It has been revealed that organoids were dissociated using TrypLE Express (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and resuspended at 40 million cells per ml in Advanced DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10 µM Y27632 after which 5 µl of cell suspension was plated onto each chip. Cells were allowed to settle for 1 h in a cell culture incubator, after which the chips were filled with Y27632-supplemented medium. The next day, Y27632 was removed and cells were cultured for 5 days. Chips were fixed in 4% PFA for 16 h at 4 °C, placed into 3D-printed custom histomoulds, filled with HistoGel (Thermo Fisher Scientific), embedded in paraffin and sectioned as described previously86. The samples were then processed for RNA in situ hybridization or immunofluorescence as described below.

In situ hybridization was performed using RNAscope technology (Advanced Cell Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. In brief, organoids were fixed in 4% PFA for 30 min at 37 °C, rinsed with PBS, dehydrated in a graded ethanol series and air dried. The slides were then rehydrated and 2 drops of hydrogen peroxide were added to each slide for 10 min. Primary antibodies were added and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The slides were washed and fixed with 4% PFA for 30 min at room temperature. After PBS washes, three drops of 1:15 diluted Protease Plus were added to slides and incubated for 10 min, followed by PBS washes.

RNA probes were prewarmed for 10 min at 40 °C, cooled down and added onto slides. The slides were incubated with probes for 2 h at 40 °C, washed twice with wash buffer, subjected to stepwise hybridization with amplifier solutions for 15 min each at 40 °C, followed by application of blocker solutions. Finally, samples were incubated with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies diluted in co-detection antibody diluent for 30 min at room temperature. After washes and brief incubation with DAPI, the slides were mounted in Elvanol and imaged. The following probes were used: ANXA1-c3 465411, LGR5-c2 311021, OLFM4-c1 311041, VIM-c1 310441. Images were obtained using the Zeiss LSM980 system using ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13).

Organoids were fixed in 4% PFA for 1 h at room temperature, permeabilized in 0.6% Triton X-100 for 30 min, blocked with 5% BSA and 5% goat serum in PBS for 2 h, after which primary antibodies were added in blocking solution and incubated overnight at 4 °C. After multiple washes in PBS, secondary Alexa Fluor-conjugated antibodies were added in 1% BSA, 1% goat serum for 2 h at room temperature. Organoids were then mounted in ProLong Gold (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The following primary antibodies were used: ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486, 1:1,000, overnight, 4 °C), YAP1 (Santa Cruz, sc-101199, 1:500, overnight, 4 °C), active YAP (Abcam, ab205270, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C), β-catenin (Cell Marque, 224M-14, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C), SNAIL1 (Santa Cruz, sc-271977, 1:50, overnight, 4 °C), HP1α (Cell Signaling, 2616, 1:200, overnight, 4 °C), lamin A/C (Cell Signaling, 2032, 1:200, overnight, 4 °C), SOX4 (Abcam, ab236557, 1:400, overnight, 4 °C), pSMAD2/3 (Cell Signaling, 3108, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C). Images were obtained using either the Zeiss LSM980 or Nikon Yokogawa CSU-W1 system with ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13) or NIS Elements (AR 5.41.01).

Sources indicate that to mechanically compress the organoids, organoids grown in Matrigel for 5 days were replated on top of Matrigel-coated 12–20 mm round glass coverslips and allowed to attach for 24 h. After attachment, the organoids were sandwiched with another 12–20 mm coverslip with a weight applying 200 Pa of vertical stress (generating a 45% reduction in organoid height) for 20 h.

For 3D organoid imaging, single cells were first embedded in 8 mg ml−1 Matrigel and, after 4 days of culture, were transferred either to fresh Matrigel or pH-adjusted 1 mg ml−1 collagen I matrices. The organoids were treated with 5 µM TDI-011536 (MedChemExpress, HY-150042), 10 ng ml−1 TGFβ1 (StemCell Technologies, 78067.1) or both with daily medium replenishment while being live-cell imaged every 30 min with a Sartorius Incucyte S3 incubator microscope for up to 4 days.

It has been revealed that bright-field images were segmented using Cellpose4-SAM87 and edge detection followed by morphological gap-closing and hole-filling to obtain binary organoid masks that were imported to ImageJ (Fiji). MorphoLibJ88 was used to quantify convexity, Geodesic diameter, Geodesic elongation and organoid area that were scaled between 0 and 1 to initially classify the organoids into expanded, dispersive or cohesive classes in an unbiased manner. As the resolution of the masks was not sufficient to accurately capture surface structures, the classifications were all manually inspected further and assigned to the final classes.

RNA was isolated using the NucleoSpin RNA plus Kit (Macherey-Nagel). RNA quality was assessed using the high-sensitivity RNA Screen Tape Analysis (TapeStation, Agilent) and subsequently 500 ng of RNA was reverse transcribed applying the SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. PCR was performed using the PowerUp SYBR Green Mastermix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on the QuantStudio5 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Gene expression was quantified using the ΔΔCt method with normalization to B2M. The following primers were used. B2M: forward primer, GAGTATGCCTGCCGTGTGAA; reverse primer, GCTTACATGTCTCGATCCCACT; AXIN2: forward primer, GCGCTGACGGATGATTCCAT; reverse primer, TGGGTTCTCGGGAAATGAGGT; ASCL2: forward primer, CGCCTACTCGTCGGACGACAG; reverse primer, GCCGCTCGCTCGGCTTCCG.

Mouse colonoscopy was performed using the TELE PACK+VET system (Karl Storz, RP101S1). Illumination was provided by a xenon light source connected through the Adapt. KST fibre-optic light cable/Xenon 100 (495KS). The system includes a camera control, air insufflation units and an integrated endoscopic video unit with built-in documentation and memory storage. Colonoscopy imaging was performed using an integrated multipurpose Hopkins Telescope (67031BA) with an outer diameter of 11.5 Fr. Images were acquired using an IMAGE1 S HX FULL HD Camera Head (TH110). Mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane and organoid fragments corresponding to 5 × 105 single cells were transplanted into the colonic submucosa using a Hamilton syringe (Hamilton, Reno, 7656-01) equipped with a transfer needle for sample loading (7770-02) and an injection needle (7803-05). The needle was carefully inserted into the colonic submucosa, and 50 µl of organoid fragments suspended in 1 mg ml−1 rat collagen type 1 (Sigma-Aldrich, C3867) supplemented with 10% Corning Matrigel (Corning, 356231) was delivered and generated a visible submucosal bleb. The mice were treated for 5 days after transplantation with the LATS kinase inhibitor TDI-011536 (MedChemExpress, HY-150042). TDI-011536 was prepared at a concentration of 5 mg ml−1 by emulsification in 10% Kolliphor HS 15 (Merck, 42966) in PBS and administered by oral gavage twice daily at a dose of 2.5 mg per kg. Vehicle-treated animals received 10% Kolliphor in PBS alone.

TGFβ1 treatment was performed using human recombinant TGFβ1 (StemCell Technologies, 78067.1) within Affi-Gel Blue beads (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 153-7301). In brief, beads were washed four times with ice-cold bi-distilled water and incubated overnight with 500 µl of 50 µg ml−1 TGFβ1 in PBS supplemented with 10 mM HEPES. TGFβ1-loaded beads were mixed with organoid fragments in collagen solution at a final proportion of 10% (v/v) before implantation. For dual-treatment experiments, animals received both TDI-011536 administration and TGFβ1-loaded beads as described above. Each treatment group consisted of four mice (n = 4). Mice were monitored three times per week, and colonoscopy imaging was performed every 2 weeks for 4 weeks before euthanasia.

Tissue biopsies (intestinal rolls) were fixed in 4% PFA, embedded in paraffin and sectioned. Sections were de-paraffinized using a graded alcohol series and antigen retrieval was carried out using target retrieval solution (Dako) at pH 6 or pH 9 in a pressure cooker. Unspecific binding was blocked using 5% normal goat serum, 3% BSA in PBS, after which antibodies were diluted in DAKO antibody diluent and incubated overnight in a moist chamber at 4 °C. After PBS washes, Alexa-Fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies were diluted in 1% BSA in PBS, incubated for 1 h at room temperature, after which samples were mounted in Elvanol. The following primary antibodies were used: ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486), pSMAD2/3 (Cell Signaling, 3108) and active YAP (Abcam ab205270). Images were obtained using the Zeiss LSM980 system with ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13). The tumour area was quantified using ANXA1 staining to generate a ROI mask in Fiji. The number of ROIs was used to extract the lesion number.

All animal experiments were performed in accordance with EU Directive 2010/63/EU and Finnish legislation, and were approved by the National Animal Experiment Board of Finland (ELLA) under project licence ESAVI/30305/2023. Female NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 005557) were used at 12 weeks of age at the start of the experiment. Sample size was determined using the resource equation method (E = N − T), where N is the total number of animals and T the number of groups; with four groups of four mice (N = 16), E = 12, within the recommended range of 10–20. Mice were randomly allocated to experimental groups; no formal randomization method was used. Tumour implantation was confirmed in all mice, and animals were euthanized and dissected 4 weeks after transplantation. No mice reached the humane end-point limits defined in the licence, and no mice were excluded from the analysis.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad, v.9) or in R (v.2023.09.1+494). Statistical significance was determined using the specific tests indicated in the corresponding figure legends. Only two-tailed tests were used. In all cases in which a test for normally distributed data was used, normal distribution was confirmed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (α = 0.05). All experiments presented in the manuscript were repeated at least in three independent replicates. Automated software algorithms were used for unbiased quantification of staining intensities, sequencing data and architecture features/cell shapes in all experiments involving these techniques so blinding was not relevant. For animal experiments endoscopy and sample collection were performed in a blinded manner. For manual organoid invasion pattern classification blinding was applied during data analysis. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Sample size was determined based on previous experience, published literature, or to specific requirements of a given technique.

All patient-related data (TMA and spatial transcriptomics post-hoc staining) have been deposited in the Helsinki Biobank (HBP20210170) and Finnish Hematology and Registry Biobank FHRB (12.5.2022). 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lewis Blain | 27 Nov 2026 07:57.

Manchester United could be handed a significant opportunity to strengthen their attack in January, with one of Mauricio Pochettino’s leading striker targets potentially now available.

AS Monaco are mentioned to be 'desperate' to sell former Arsenal forward Folarin Balogun as they look to balance their books, potentially opening the door for the Red Devils to reignite their interest.

United are expected to prioritise three positions during the winter transfer window, with a new centre-forward, left-back and centre-back reportedly on Pochettino’s wishlist.

Industry observers note that balogun is among the strikers under consideration, with the new Man Utd manager already familiar with the USA international from their time together with the national team. The forward was arguably Pochettino’s star player at the 2026 World Cup.

United could have an opportunity to make their move after journalist Ben Jacobs, speaking to The United Stand, claimed the Ligue 1 side need to sell either Balogun or midfielder Lamine Camara in January to balance their finances.

“Monaco desperately have to sell and will have to lose one of Balogun or Camara in January,” he remarked.

Balogun came close to joining Everton in the summer, even travelling to Merseyside on deadline day before the proposed transfer collapsed. The Toffees could revisit their interest, although Jacobs suggested the race for his signature could be wide open.

United are also considering other options, including Victor Osimhen and Ivan Toney, but a January move for the former is considered extremely difficult.

Balogun, meanwhile, has scored twice in nine appearances across all competitions since returning from an injury that initially contributed to his failed Everton move.

United's reported transfer budget of less than £50m remains a significant obstacle, particularly with Pochettino also keen to strengthen at left-back and centre-back.

Monaco's willingness to sell could improve United's negotiating position, but it does not necessarily mean Balogun would represent a bargain. The club must also consider whether he is the right option to provide the immediate goals required.

Benjamin Sesko's persistent shin injury and Joshua Zirkzee's uncertain future have increased the need for another centre-forward, but Balogun's return of just two goals in nine games hardly makes him a guaranteed solution.

If Monaco are prepared to accept a relatively modest fee, United should seriously consider the opportunity.

However, with several positions requiring attention and limited funds available, Pochettino cannot afford to spend a significant proportion of his January budget on another forward who arrives with questions over his current form.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, unfortunately for Chelsea, Wesley Fofana put his hand up twice.
  • Sources indicate that and secondly to volunteer to take one of the penalties in the shoot-out.
  • LIVERPOOL ARE THROUGH TO THE QUARTER-FINALS OF THE CARABAO CUP!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, unfortunately for Chelsea, Wesley Fofana put his hand up twice. Firstly to concede the first-half penalty for handball that allowed Liverpool to equalise quickly after Chelsea themselves had scored from the spot.

Sources indicate that and secondly to volunteer to take one of the penalties in the shoot-out. The defender had to score to keep Chelsea in it, but he woefully, nervously skied his effort high into a gleeful Kop and it was Liverpool who went through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.

LIVERPOOL ARE THROUGH TO THE QUARTER-FINALS OF THE CARABAO CUP! 🔴 Wesley Fofana blazes over to hand Liverpool their FIFTH consecutive victory ✅ https://t.co/M4n01R8DSk.

There the reward for Andoni Iraola, the head coach, is a home tie against the club he left in the summer: Bournemouth. The draw has opened up for Liverpool, and they know it, with only Manchester City left of the other big guns. But despite again playing at Anfield, they would have preferred not to face such a dangerous and motivated opponent, who have just reeled off five wins and five clean sheets in a row under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose.

Recent findings suggest that this was also a big win. A meaningful win. One that was celebrated as such with Dua Lipa’s One Kiss – an anthem on Jürgen Klopp’s run to Liverpool’s first Champions League final under him in 2018 – played over the loudspeakers at the end as the players joyfully milled around the pitch.

One kiss is all it takes 🎶 https://t.co/0jfujy4V94.

Recent findings suggest that “I am happy to feel it. We feel the support,” Iraola said when asked whether he sensed the momentum and togetherness building in his reshaped Liverpool side. It looks as though they are.

Fofana was Chelsea’s eighth taker, so they were running out of options, but it was a truly terrible effort. The 25-year-old turned and scratched his head – just as many Chelsea fans have done over his underwhelming, albeit injury-hit, contributions since his eyebrow-raising £75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

Industry observers note that both sides had the chance to win it earlier in the shoot-out. For Liverpool it was Kostas Tsimikas, who had taken the decisive kick to beat Chelsea in a shoot-out in the 2022 FA Cup final, but the Greek full-back also completely missed the target.

Tsimikas has the chance to put Liverpool through... And fires over the bar! 😱 https://t.co/eCKBT6njMB.

Sources indicate that then Chelsea striker Emmanuel Emegha – on his debut – saw his kick saved, after an effort by Ryan Gravenberch had also been stopped. In the end, Liverpool’s stand-in captain Joe Gomez – still to score an actual goal – crashed in his kick before Fofana’s blunder. The 29-year-old Gomez finally “scored” and it was an assured strike.

This was the fifth penalty shoot-out between these two clubs, in all competitions, with Liverpool having now triumphed in all five. They won the toss for this one and elected to take the kicks in front of the Kop, which roared its satisfaction and did its best to unsettle the Chelsea takers.

Both stand-in goalkeepers – Giorgi Mamardashvili and Mike Penders – made one outstanding save each in the shoot-out. Chelsea substitute Valentín Barco was the other player to miss, hitting a post.

In a recent development, chelsea blink first in the shootout! 🔵 Valentín Barco's penalty bounces off the post... https://t.co/rSXGfQctbI.

According to recent reports, the other efforts, in truth, were outstanding and assured with Liverpool, undoubtedly, benefitting from Iraola turning to his bench and bringing on Alexander Isak, Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. All scored their penalties.

Among Chelsea’s scorers was Jordan Henderson and the former Liverpool captain received a strange homecoming in his first appearance at Anfield for three years. He was booed, in the first half at least, and especially when he tucked the ball under his arm before Chelsea took their penalty – in normal time – which gave them the lead. Henderson turned to the stands, grinning.

Morgan Rogers buries the spotkick! ⚽️ Chelsea take the lead at Anfield 🔵 https://t.co/YlDn2gakRi.

In truth it was more pantomime than meaningful and Henderson, like another former, Champions League-winning Liverpool midfielder Xabi Alonso – now Chelsea’s head coach – did not celebrate as Morgan Rogers scored. The penalty came after a rash challenge by Gravenberch, who crashed into Moisés Caicedo as the Chelsea captain ran on to Malo Gusto’s shrewd reverse pass inside the area.

Afterwards, Alonso faced more questions about his decision not to use Estêvão Willian. Despite injury to João Pedro and Cole Palmer’s suspension, there was only a place on the Chelsea bench for the 19-year-old Brazilian. And he stayed there even though Alonso used all five substitutions. It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola mentioned ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”.

In a recent development, giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Recent findings suggest that like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso said. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”.

In a recent development, former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

In a recent development, the Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AC Milan head coach Ruben Amorim believes that the comeback win over Olympiacos is something that could ‘change the future’.

After 50 minutes of the game on the outskirts of Athens, it looked like Milan were heading for a fourth defeat in five Europa League games. Lorenzo Pirola crashed a header in off the bar via Mike Maignan, then Jota Silva scored a second early in the second half.

In a recent development, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Recent findings suggest that then, out of almost nowhere, Omari Hutchinson inspired a run of three goals in 15 minutes. Firstly he scored a goal of his own with a brilliant solo run, then he set up Alphadjo Cisse for his 10th goal of the season, then he crossed for a Christian Pulisic volley to make it 3-2.

Diego Moreira added a fourth late on to make sure of the points. Amorim spoke to Sky after the final whistle to give his thoughts on what was a rollercoaster night, but one that thankfully ended well. His words are via MilanNews.

Will this second half change the Europa League season?

“It definitely changes our future. We played well in the second half, but we made a lot of mistakes again and we need to improve. But we got a lot of players back, it was a positive night.”.

It has been revealed that “It’s better to finish games like this, winning obviously. We have a lot of work to do to be a very strong team, but the spirit is there. It’s the start of something.”.

“I think this is the biggest problem: focusing on the small details like set pieces, goalkeeping, and the plays we need to make. It comes with time and experience.

Sources indicate that “The technical aspect is fine, but concentration is the most important thing. It’s tough to play physically every three days, but it’s even tougher to constantly have this pressure of having to win.”.

“I always expect this. He has the potential to do much more. He’s talented, like other players on the team. It’s no surprise, he’s very talented. It’s the mentality that counts.”.

How do you explain the build-up errors?

“We lost the ball without being pressured, trying to play the ball. We left Jashari alone to set up a team with four of our players behind their midfielders. When we had the ball, we gave it away without pressure.

“Koni sometimes put the ball in areas where there was pressure, but instead he was supposed to carry the ball. He’s responsible for pushing the team forward and guiding us forward. We went to get into their pressing zones.”.

It’s your first comeback win of the season….

“I think it’s a great feeling. If you look at the Benfica match, we had several opportunities. We created more than today. You have to see it to believe it, and today we saw that we came from two goals behind and won 4-2. Our confidence will grow.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ronald Araujo's Liverpool future is still up in the air.

The defender has been top class for the Reds since he joined them in the summer and, although it took him a couple of games to get into Iraola's prepares, he's now earned himself a guaranteed place in his starting XI.

Indeed, he is being used as a right-back which isn't his natural position but, he's that good in both positions that it doesn't really matter where he's played.

He helps bring an extra layer of defensive stability to Anfield and he's also helped shore up their back line massively.

This has allowed Jeremy Jacquet the time to adjust to Premier League life and has ensured that he was one of the best defensive transfers made in the summer.

But, since Liverpool's option to buy the midfielder is rather high at €55 million, alternative options are now making their way onto the Reds' shortlist.

Liverpool can sign Mohamed Simakan for €35 million.

Right-back has been a problem area for Liverpool ever since they got rid of Trent Alexander-Arnold last summer.

Jeremie Frimpong was brought in to try and help plug the gap while Conor Bradley was expected to take over as Liverpool's first choice right-back.

But, thanks to the injuries that both players suffered, the Reds' looks didn't work out exactly as they wanted them to which resulted in Araujo being signed this summer.

As mentioned, the Uruguayan has been in fine form this term but, since he's not an actual Liverpool player, a decision needs to be made on his future.

But, with the way that things seem to be going, Araujo looks likely to return to Barcelona.

This has led to fans asking many questions about who their starting right-back is going to be with Caught Offside now throwing a newly introduced defender into the mix.

"Liverpool, Manchester United, Arsenal, Tottenham and Newcastle have all continued scouting Simakan, although no formal offers or advanced negotiations have taken place," they wrote.

"For Liverpool, Simakan’s versatility is particularly attractive.

"With long-term succession planning required in central defence, signing a player capable of operating centrally while also covering right-back would give the squad valuable flexibility.

"The asking price will be crucial. At €35m-€40m, Simakan would represent a relatively manageable investment compared with some of the €70m-plus defenders presently being linked with both clubs.

"There are still questions about adapting back to European football after his spell in Saudi Arabia, but at 26 he should be entering his peak years.".

Mohamed Simakan can cover all the positions Ronald Araujo does for Liverpool.

Not only is Mohamed Simakan younger than Araujo but, he's also worth a lot less.

€35 million for a 26-year-old in this market is unheard of, especially for a versatile defender such as the Frenchman.

As Caught Offside mention, his last couple of years being spent in Saudi Arabia do pose a bit of a worry but, within a few months of making a return to European football, he should be able to get back to his best.

The main stumbling block between Liverpool and Barcelona for an Araujo deal is the fee that the La Liga outfit want.

So, the fact that Simakan is younger, can play in all the positions that Araujo covers for Liverpool and the fact that he'd be cheaper for them to buy, makes a deal for the Frenchman a no-brainer.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.
  • Industry observers note that these themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's fresh album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday.
  • Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he reveals little sign of putting down his guitar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

Industry observers note that these themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's fresh album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he reveals little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the concerns shaping the world today.

It has been revealed that in his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

Recent findings suggest that this outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

Industry observers note that wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly noted in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

In a recent development, yet Biermann has said his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama.".

Recent findings suggest that biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism.".

It has been revealed that in 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Recent findings suggest that biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann noted. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer.".

In a recent development, in 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. ".

Industry observers note that I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Recent findings suggest that afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he noted.

According to recent reports, he became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he noted. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom.".

According to recent reports, the singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he stated, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

Industry observers note that "I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

Sources indicate that and should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

This article was originally written in German.

Manchester City are continuing to invest in young talent as they look to strengthen their squad for the future, with another exciting prospect emerging on their transfer radar.

Pep Guardiola’s side have reportedly moved into pole position for one of Borussia Dortmund’s most highly rated youngsters.

United States international Mathis Albert has attracted interest from several European clubs, but City are right now considered the favourites to secure his signature.

With the teenager’s first-team opportunities limited in Germany, the Premier League champions could look to take advantage of the situation.

According to TEAMtalk, Manchester City are the frontrunners to sign Albert after making a formal approach during the summer transfer window.

The report claims City are prepared to offer the 17-year-old lucrative personal terms as they step up their pursuit. Their interest is serious, with the club previously prepared to meet a valuation in the region of €20 million (£16.7m).

Chelsea are also long-term admirers of the youngster and were reportedly willing to spend a similar amount last winter. Paris Saint-Germain previously made contact with Dortmund in 2025, while Arsenal and Liverpool have more recently been monitoring his situation.

However, City are currently viewed as being in the strongest position should Dortmund soften their stance.

Recent findings suggest that albert joined Borussia Dortmund from the LA Galaxy academy in 2024 and has promptly established himself as one of the most exciting young American talents in European football. He has already made Bundesliga appearances and earned senior international recognition with the United States.

Despite his potential, opportunities under Niko Kovac have been limited this season. That lack of regular first-team football has encouraged several clubs to monitor his development, although Dortmund remain determined to keep hold of their young attacker.

According to recent reports, the Bundesliga side have reportedly rejected approaches, including loan enquiries, and continue to view Albert as an crucial part of their long-term plans. They are also preparing a contract extension offer, with his current agreement running until June 2027.

There is another crucial factor for City. Premier League regulations prevent English clubs from signing Albert permanently until he turns 18 in May, meaning any potential transfer would be geared towards next summer rather than an immediate move.
