According to recent reports, we found that targeting the AMOTL2 TSS led to a complete knockdown of AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs and human coronary artery endothelial cells (HCAECs) (Fig. 5c). Importantly, targeting the rs9876658-containing enhancer reduced AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs but not HCAECs, bolstering our prediction (Fig. 5c). Collectively, these analyses nominate rs9876658 as a causal regulator of AMOTL2 expression in SMCs but not endothelial cells and implicate this gene as a fresh candidate gene for atherosclerosis through an effect in SMCs. To dissect the functional impact of targeting AMOTL2 in HCASMCs, we compared non-targeting control and AMOTL2 knockdown HCASMCs. We observed disordered cellular morphology as well as decreased calponin (CNN1) and alpha-smooth muscle actin (ACTA2) expression by immunofluorescence in AMOTL2 knockdown cells, suggesting a shift away from the quiescent contractile state (Fig. 5d). We performed bulk RNA sequencing in stressed non-targeting control and AMOTL2 knockdown cells (Fig. 5e). Gene ontology pathway analysis revealed an upregulation of cell-cycle-related genes and a downregulation of cell-motility-associated pathways (Fig. 5f). Consistent with our immunofluorescence staining (Fig. 5d), we saw a reduction in contractile SMC gene expression (ACTA2, CNN1, TAGLN and LMOD1) in AMOTL2 knockdown cells relative to control (Fig. 5g). Finally, AMOTL2 knockdown cells had a significantly greater proliferation rate (Fig. 5h). Taken together, these findings establish a functional role for AMOTL2 in SMC proliferation and migration—pathways integral in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.

Although GWAS have identified hundreds of CAD-associated variants1,5,28,29, translation to therapies remains limited by incomplete understanding of the causal cell types and gene programmes30,31. The emergence of multi-omic single-cell technologies has created a unique opportunity to profile human tissue at unprecedented resolution14,32. Numerous studies have leveraged these technologies to uncover cellular heterogeneity in human tissue across many diseases, contributing to a human cell atlas17,18,24,33. Few studies have mapped common disease variants to causal cell types and target genes directly in human tissue, with previous work limited by unimodal profiling or cell-based systems that lack the native tissue context.

Our study used a new technique—single-nucleus multi-ome (RNA+ATAC)—in human coronary arteries from 44 patients with paired genotyping for unbiased characterization of the transcriptome and epigenome at single-cell resolution. Capturing paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility from the same nucleus allows for more robust peak-gene linkage21 and represents an important milestone for regulatory biology of the human vasculature. We also used a new computational framework—scE2G21—to build an unbiased genome-wide scE2G map in human CAD. Notably, our scV2E2G framework identified a substantial set of CAD-associated enhancer–gene links in SMCs, including 325 linked genes, providing a basis for downstream functional interrogation of SMC regulatory programmes. This systematic approach can be applied broadly across diseases and allows for an unbiased framework to prioritize pathological genes and cell types driving common heritable human diseases.

To nominate functional regulatory variants in a broader cohort, we integrated our data with published human coronary artery snATAC–seq19 to identify 11,269 sc-caQTLs, enabling QTL discovery in cell types that are obscured in bulk analyses34,35. Mechanistic dissection of rs658956 illustrates how non-coding CAD variants can act through cell-type-specific disruption of transcription factor binding and enhancer activity36. The disruption of an AP-1 (JUN/FOS) motif by this variant is particularly notable given the well-established role of AP-1 in SMC phenotypic switching and the recent evidence that AP-1 family members act as pioneer factors governing vascular cell chromatin landscapes37 and carry epigenetic memory of inflammation38. Furthermore, SMC-specific regulation of the lncRNA FGGY-DT highlights the potential contribution of cell-restricted non-coding RNA programmes to cardiovascular disease39,40,41, although its downstream role remains to be defined.

Traditional pseudobulk QTL discovery lacks the ability to discriminate between molecular traits that are influenced by disease state3. Here we used single-cell genomics to define cell-state dynamics in one of the most fluid cell types in the atherosclerotic plaque. In atherosclerosis, contractile SMCs undergo de-differentiation and acquire an FMC phenotype with distinct transcriptional signatures16. We applied a continuous score reflecting SMC to FMC transition to map dynamic caQTLs that are dependent on cell-state. Using this framework, we uncovered rs658956 as a caQTL for FGGY-DT enhancer that is associated with altered activity as SMCs transition to FMCs. This is an application of single-cell-state-dependent QTL modelling in human cardiovascular disease and expands our understanding of gene regulation in heterogeneous cell states.

According to recent reports, we applied arrayed Perturb–seq42 to GWAS-nominated enhancers and their SMC-linked target genes, enabling transcriptome-wide functional validation of non-coding regulatory elements and their downstream gene programmes. Critically, the arrayed format preserves non-cell-autonomous transcriptional effects that can be obscured in pooled screens where shared culture conditions confound intrinsic regulatory responses through paracrine signalling, as in a recent CAD variant-to-gene-to-programme framework26. The convergence of several enhancer perturbations on inflammatory and ECM-remodelling programmes is consistent with the established role of said processes in atherosclerosis, including induction of matrix metalloproteinases and collagens43. Together, these data support a model in which CAD variants act through cell-type-specific enhancers to co-ordinately dysregulate inflammation, ECM homeostasis and proliferation during transition from contractile SMCs to pathological FMCs18,44.

Given that the genome is organized as a dynamic 3D structure45, chromatin looping through topologically associating domains (TADs) represents a higher-order regulatory layer governing gene expression45,46. Although Hi-C has been used in cell-based systems and other tissues to map chromatin architecture and connect disease variants to distal genes47,48, large-scale chromatin structures are highly tissue- and cell-type-specific27,48,49 and remain unexplored in diseased human arterial tissue. Here, genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries enabled tissue-specific mapping of chromatin networks and distal variant–gene interactions. Notably, we discovered that rs4887091 creates an allele-specific CTCF binding site with dosage-dependent effects on both CTCF occupancy and loop strength, defining a mechanistically distinct non-coding regulatory mechanism involving 3D genome architecture48. Haplotype-resolved analysis confirmed the allele-specific increase in looping strength50,51, consistent with recent demonstrations that phased Hi-C can resolve allele-specific chromatin structure at disease loci52 and that variants within CTCF sites can alter looping and gene regulation in a dosage-sensitive manner50,51. The linked gene, ADAMTS7, is causally implicated in CAD, with Adamts7 deficiency reducing atherosclerosis and its catalytic activity regulating SMC migration53,54. Although our data do not establish altered looping as the proximal mechanism controlling ADAMTS7 expression, allele-dependent changes to chromatin architecture may represent a previously unrecognized regulatory mechanism at this locus.

Furthermore, our tissue Hi-C framework enabled systematic genome-wide nomination of distal causal genes. We identified 11 genes linked to CAD variants through chromatin contacts, most of which, for example AMOTL2, were not the gene nearest to the disease-associated variant. CRISPRi targeting of the enhancer linked distally to AMOTL2 reduced AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs but not HCAECs, and AMOTL2 knockdown in HCASMCs increased cellular proliferation and suppressed contractile marker expression, consistent with a shift away from a quiescent state. This phenotype aligns with the known function of AMOTL2 as a scaffold protein55,56 that retains YAP in the cytoplasm to suppress Hippo-driven proliferative transcription, such that its loss de-represses YAP nuclear activity and promotes cell-cycle progression57. The connection between a CAD-associated variant and a Hippo pathway regulator with established roles in vascular cell proliferation and mechanosensing58,59 points to dysregulation of YAP and/or TAZ signalling in SMCs as a potentially underappreciated axis in atherosclerotic disease.

Sources indicate that our study has several limitations. First, nuclear RNA provides more limited cell-state resolution than whole-cell RNA, so we leveraged high-resolution published single-cell data for reference mapping and state imputation. Second, caQTL discovery remains constrained by sample size, cell abundance and allele frequency, limiting power in rarer cell types and variants and complicating interpretation of differences in caQTLs across cell types. Residual population stratification in our multi-ancestry cohort may have also resulted in false positives, although our summary statistics can support future meta-analyses in larger cohorts. Third, multi-ome profiling does not capture post-transcriptional regulation such as alternative splicing. Finally, bulk coronary Hi-C precludes genome-wide cell-type-specific looping inference; we therefore used targeted Hi-ChIP–seq for cell-type resolution at selected loci. Although CRISPRi Perturb–seq supports ADAMTS7 as a responsive target of the rs4887091-containing enhancer, direct allele editing or CTCF motif perturbation will be required to establish whether allele-dependent looping causally regulates ADAMTS7 expression.

It has been revealed that in conclusion, we built a multi-omic gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility map of human CAD and provide a comprehensive framework to map CAD GWAS variants to causal genes and affected cell types. Furthermore, we use pseudobulk and single-cell QTL modelling to characterize state-dependent and independent regulatory mechanism of disease variants in human tissue. We used tissue Hi-C to build large-scale chromatin networks and uncover how disease variants impact distal gene regulation. Finally, we integrated tissue -omics with in vitro epigenetic profiling to prioritize and functionally test candidate genes using Perturb–seq and CRISPRi. Collectively, we provide a disease agnostic framework to apply human genetic findings to nominate pathologic cell states and genes driving disease, constructing a comprehensive GWAS variant-to-gene map with genetic- and tissue-level convergence for future mechanistic and therapeutic studies.

The study is compliant with all relevant ethical regulations and has been approved by the Washington University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board (no. 201104172). Informed consent was obtained from each patient before tissue collection by Washington University School of Medicine; no compensation was provided in exchange for participation in the study, and participants consented to publication of research data. Written consent was obtained. Demographic data have been de-identified and are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Patients included in this study span diverse race, age and sex to provide an inclusive trans-ethnic study population.

Before tissue collection, specific inclusion criteria were used to ensure well controlled study groups. Any patients with human immunodeficiency virus or hepatitis and known genetic cardiomyopathies were excluded from this study. The left anterior descending coronary artery was isolated, and flash frozen from donor hearts (patients with stable ejection fractions who experienced non-cardiac cause of death) and from patients with chronic heart failure (ischaemic and non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy) at the time of heart transplantation. For all samples, the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery was used. All demographic and clinical data have been de-identified and are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Recruitment was therefore determined by donor and/or transplant tissue availability and clinical indication rather than population-based sampling, which may limit generalizability to the broader CAD population.

In a recent development, the left anterior descending coronary artery was dissected from explanted hearts; epicardial fat was removed, and arteries were flash frozen using liquid nitrogen. Identical regions from the proximal left anterior descending artery were used from all patients. Single-nuclei suspensions were generated as described previously17. Nuclei were isolated according to the 10x Genomics protocol (Nuclei Isolation Complex Sample for ATAC GEX Sequencing RevB, CG000375) and flow cytometry for 7-AAD (Sigma, SML1633-1ML) positive nuclei was used for sorting using a BD FACS Melody (BD Biosciences) with a 100-µm nozzle. Protocol CG000338 from 10x Genomics was used for Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multi-ome ATAC + Gene Expression. Briefly, following nuclei isolation, permeabilization was performed, followed by transposition, GEM generation and barcoding using ChipJ (10x Genomics, PN1000234), post-GEM clean up, pre-amplification PCR, cDNA amplification, library construction and sequencing. Gene-expression and ATAC libraries were sequenced to a read depth of 50,000 and 25,000, respectively, using a NovaSeq 6000 platform (Illumina) at the McDonnell Genome Institute. Data were acquired and sorted using BD FACSChorus v.1.1.

Sources indicate that raw fastq files were aligned to the human GRCh38 reference genome using CellRanger ARC (10x Genomics, v.6.1), with ATAC data processed in ArchR (v.1.0.3)60 and RNA data in Seurat (v.5.5.1). After quality control, doublet removal, SCTransform normalization (sctransform v.0.4.3)61, Harmony integration (v.2.0.5)62, clustering and RNA-based cell-type annotation, RNA annotations were transferred to the paired ATAC profiles. Detailed quality control thresholds and clustering procedures are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1.

We used the scE2GMulti-ome model21 to predict enhancer–gene connections in 11 cell types from 10x Genomics multi-ome data. In each cell type, scE2G scores every candidate element–gene pair (where candidate elements are ATAC peaks within 5 Mb of the TSS of the gene) by integrating several features. Regulatory enhancer–gene interactions were defined as element–gene pairs with a score greater than 0.171.

According to recent reports, the scE2Gmulti-ome model is a supervised classifier adapted for multi-omic data from ENCODE-rE2G63. It integrates eight features, including (1) a pseudobulk activity-by-contact score, where 3D contact is estimated by an inverse function of genomic distance; (2) the Kendall correlation across single cells between element accessibility and gene expression; (3) whether the gene is ‘expressed ubiquitously’ and (4) several other measures of genomic distance and chromatin accessibility around the element and promoter. The score threshold of 0.171 was determined as the score yielding 70% recall when evaluating predictions in K562 cells against CRISPRi-validated enhancer–gene pairs.

Sources indicate that scE2G predictions for all cell types can be found in Supplementary Tables 3–14. To construct the disease-relevant scV2E2G map, we selected ATAC–seq peaks from the four main cell types that contained a CAD GWAS variant, defined cell-type-specific enhancers by overlap with coronary artery H3K27ac peaks, linked these enhancers to genes using scE2G and finally overlapped scE2G peaks with sc-caQTLs to nominate links supported by a molecular trait.

To test for enrichment of disease risk in the four main cell types, stratified LDSC64 was used to partition heritability in cell-type marker peaks. First, cell-type specific marker peaks (FDR < 0.01, log2[fold change] > 1) were obtained using ArchR (v.1.0.3) and converted to GRCh37 coordinates using liftover65. GWAS summary statistics for CAD1, diabetes66, abdominal aortic aneurysms67, DBP and SBP68, and stroke 69 were obtained, and their formats were standardized using MungeSumstats (v.1.20.0)70. Stratified LD score analysis (LDSC v.1.0.1) was then carried out with --h2-cts flag for cell-type specific analyses. P values obtained from stratified LDSC were considered significant for a condition if they were lower than Bonferroni-corrected P value threshold of 8.33 × 10−3 (for six conditions tested). To examine overlap between CAD GWAS variants and ATAC peaks, lead variants from 241 genome-wide significant (P < 5 × 10−8) loci and 897 conditionally independent variants meeting FDR cutoff (FDR < 0.01) were obtained from Aragam and colleagues1. Additional variants that are in high linkage disequilibrium (r2 > 0.80 within 250 kb) with these lead variants were obtained from the 1000 Genomes European panel using PLINK v.1.9 --tag-r2 flag. Furthermore, these variants were combined with the functional fine-mapped credible set variants from Aragam and colleagues1 to create a superset of GWAS variants to be tested for overlap. These variants were overlapped with ATAC peak regions using the findOverlaps function in the IRanges R package (v.2.46.0).

According to recent reports, to obtain high-quality genotypes from patients, DNA from peripheral leukocytes of 39 participants was genotyped using Illumina GSA-24-V3 SNP array. Following initial processing using Illumina GenomeStudio software v.2.0.5, variants with both (1) minor allele frequency (MAF) >5% and call rate <95% or (2) MAF <5% and call rate <99% were excluded. No patients were excluded by the call rate exclusion filter (<95%). Additional genotypes were further imputed from the TOPMED panel on the Michigan Imputation Server v.1.7.1 using minimac v.4-1.0.2 (ref. 71) and phasing with Eagle v.2.4.1 (ref. 72). Following imputation, variants with imputation R2 > 0.3 and MAF > 0.05 were further kept for caQTL analysis for a final dataset containing 7,250,405 variants. To conduct combined caQTL mapping, the variant call format (VCF) files from Turner and colleagues19 were merged with the imputed genotype dataset, and shared SNPs in only two datasets were kept for downstream analysis. Turner and colleagues carried out low-coverage whole-genome sequencing; further details are available in the original publication19. Following the merge, 5,229,397 variants were available for QTL analysis. Local ancestries were inferred using RFMix v.2.03-r0 with default settings73. Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria (YRI, n = 186) and Utah residents with ancestry from northern and western Europe (CEU, n = 183) from the 1000 Genomes Project74 were used as African and/or European reference populations, respectively.

It has been revealed that to achieve uniform cell-type annotations across datasets, snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues19 were reference mapped onto the multi-ome dataset rather than integrated. Raw snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues were downloaded and reprocessed using identical quality control thresholds (minimum fragment count and TSS enrichment cut-offs) as applied to the multi-ome snATAC–seq, ensuring consistent data processing upstream of annotation. Gene activity scores were computed from the snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues using ArchR (v.1.0.3)60 and used as the query, with the snRNA-seq component of the multi-ome data serving as the reference for label transfer through Seurat’s anchor-based framework (v.5.5.1). This approach leveraged the higher-quality transcriptomic annotations from the multi-ome dataset to annotate the external snATAC–seq data without merging the two datasets. Annotation concordance between transferred labels and author-provided annotations from Turner and colleagues19 was assessed using Jaccard Index across the four main cell populations used for QTL mapping.

Similar to previous studies for sc-caQTL discovery19,75, we used RASQUAL76 to identify pseudobulk caQTLs in four main cell types (SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts). RASQUAL v.1.1 was chosen as our mapping method due to its ability to simultaneously model allelic imbalance and count-based QTL effect to improve fine-mapping of putative causal variants. RASQUAL maximizes power for caQTL discovery by simultaneously modelling allelic imbalance and total read counts in each locus. To generate fragment counts within each ATAC peak regions, we loaded each fragment object and used Signac (v.1.17.1) FeatureMatrix function to generate a cell-by-peak count matrix for all cells within each cell type. This matrix was subsequently aggregated at a sample pseudobulk level using rollup function from the R slam package (v.0.1-56). For RASQUAL’s allele-specific modelling, createASVCF.sh script in paired-read mode was used to generate allele-specific fragment counts at each site with additional BAM flag of -F 1280 to exclude secondary or PCR duplicate reads. For each cell type, only samples with at least 20 cells of that cell type and only peaks with at least five reads on average across all samples were included for the final analysis.

Sources indicate that for the caQTL association analysis, all variants within a ±10-kb cis-window of the peaks were tested for association. Total library size for each sample was included as an offset. Age, sex, sequencing site and first four principal components of genotype data (generated from plink --pca) were included as covariates. For multiple testing correction, we used the two-step correction procedure recommended by RASQUAL76, including locus-level correction followed by a genome-wide correction using an empirical null distribution generated using genotype permutations. The caQTL variants were queried subsequently in bulk eQTL datasets using Qtlizer (v.1.22.0)77. Power, MAF-stratified validation, model comparison and genotype-PC sensitivity analyses are described in Supplementary Fig. 2. For locus-level multiple testing, a Q value corresponding to SNP-level FDR was calculated using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and the SNP with the lowest Q value was selected for each locus. For genome-wide correction, an empirical null distribution was calculated from four RASQUAL runs using randomly permuted genotypes; the averaged null distribution was used to obtain Q value cut-offs corresponding to 1%, 5% and 10% genome-wide FDR.

We compared the myeloid cell caQTLs with previously published monocyte caQTLs discovered in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 15 healthy donors. We found that 26.7% (767 of 2,868) of the lead macrophage caQTL variants were also the lead variant among the previously identified 3,528 monocyte caQTLs. Although only a minority, this difference may reflect the profoundly distinct biological environments between peripheral blood mononuclear cells and myeloid cells in atherosclerotic lesions75.

Pseudobulk caQTLs for the main cell types can be found in Supplementary Tables 15–26. To assess transcription factor binding potential at caQTLs, we trained seq2PRINT22 in SMCs using chromatin accessibility and ATAC footprinting to predict transcription factor binding probability at base-pair resolution and compared caQTL variants with non-caQTL cis-SNPs within accessible peaks.

By mapping our multi-ome dataset onto a recently published coronary artery CITE-seq dataset18, we demonstrated concordant mapping scores across SMC cell states, and projecting the FMC module score into this independent dataset confirmed the score was most enriched in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In human spatial transcriptomics data, the FMC score showed greater enrichment in diseased relative to healthy coronary vessels (Extended Data Fig. 5e), and in carotid plaques the FMC score correlated positively with percent stenosis (Spearman ρ = 0.58, P = 0.019), linking FMC identity directly to disease burden (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Pseudotime trajectory analysis demonstrated progressive enrichment of the FMC score as SMCs differentiate, recapitulated by both our module and an independently published gene set (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). Using an in vitro serum starvation and replenishment model of phenotypic switching in HCASMCs followed by scRNA-seq, we confirmed that the FMC score is elevated significantly in the stressed state (Extended Data Fig. 5i). Consistent with this, published time-course murine atherosclerosis data in SMC lineage-traced cells found progressive expansion of the FMC module with disease progression (Extended Data Fig. 5j). Finally, the FMC score was correlated positively with ChromVAR-predicted activity78 of established FMC transcriptional regulators including the MEF2 family, linking chromatin remodelling to transcriptional dynamics along this differentiation axis (Extended Data Fig. 5k). Collectively, these analyses establish the reproducibility of the FMC module across independent human datasets, its association with clinical disease burden, and its relevance to both in vitro and in vivo models of SMC phenotypic switching.

According to recent reports, in addition to the pseudobulk caQTL model, we used a PME single-cell model to map caQTLs in SMCs. This approach models cell-level fragment counts with random effect covariates to account for relatedness shared by cells from the same sample and batch. Such attempts to model discrete count distributions at a single-cell level have been shown to generally boost power in single-cell QTL discovery compared with pseudobulk and/or linear regression frameworks79,80,81. Our PME model was adapted from the PME model used by Nathan and colleagues3 for single-cell eQTL mapping as follows:.

where ATAC fragment counts (A) was modelled with fixed-effect covariates (G, genotype; nFrags, number of fragments per cell, TSSEnrich, TSS enrichment per cell; accPC, principal components of single-nucleus ATAC counts; genoPC, principal components of genotype data), random effect covariates (d, donor ID; s, sequencing site) and intercept (θ). All quantitative covariates were scaled and centred before the regression analysis. Significance of the genotype effect term (βG) was tested by LRT of the full model containing the genotype term and a null model without the genotype term. Due to the high computational load of running Poisson regression analysis on all cells, this analysis was restricted to lead caQTL variants from the pseudobulk RASQUAL analysis, which models the fragment counts using a negative binomial model. All Poisson models were fit using the glmer function from the lme4 R package (v.2.0-6). We confirmed that our data is generally not over-dispersed by plotting the mean variance relationship between a random subset of peaks. Similarly, using a zero-inflated Poisson regression model or a negative binomial model on a subset of our hits revealed little differences in overall regression estimates. Given that a small proportion of our pseudobulk hits probably represent null results, we did not conduct FDR correction due to our inability to accurately estimate the proportion of results from the null distribution. Instead, we compared z values between our pseudobulk and PME models.

A key benefit of modelling individual cells instead of sample-level pseudobulk is our ability to simultaneously model cell-state covariates (for example, differentiation trajectories, gene and/or protein expression) as well as potential interaction between genotypes and cell-state covariates. We defined FMC identity score by calculating the gene activity of the top 100 FMC (modulated SMC) marker genes defined by Wirka and colleagues16 from our integrated snATAC–seq meta-map using ArchR (v.1.0.3) addGeneScoreMatrix() and Seurat (v.5.5.1) AddModuleScore(). To test for ‘dynamic’ caQTL where the genotype effect is modified by SMC cell state, we then added the FMC score and a genotype-FMC score interaction term as covariates in the following model:.

Again, this analysis was carried out just on the significant (FDR < 5%) lead variants from the pseudobulk caQTL analyses, although it is entirely possible that there are non-significant pseudobulk caQTLs (that is, genotype effect is near zero for average FMC score) that may have significant interaction terms. We obtained P values for the genotype-FMC score interaction term using an LRT. We subsequently applied Storey Q value correction to LRT P values of the interaction term across all tested variants for multiple-testing correction. Dynamic caQTLs can be found in Supplementary Tables 29 and 30.

It has been revealed that for EMSA, reference allele probe (5′-atagttcagaaacctgactcagccccttctt-3′) and alternate allele probe (5′- atagttcagaaaccttactcagccccttctt-3′) for rs658956 were synthesized and labelled with IRDye700 (Integrated DNA Technologies). The labelled (100 nM) and competitor (5 μM) probes were incubated with 5–10 μg of SMC nuclear extract in binding buffer (final concentration 8% Ficoll, 160 mM KCl, 20 mM HEPES, 10 mM MgCl2, 2.5 mM dithiothreitol, 0.25% Tween-20) and 1 μg of Poly dI*dC competitor at 4 °C for 1 h. For supershift assays, the protein complex was also incubated with anti-cJun (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-74543), anti-cFos (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-166940) or anti-JunB (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-8051) before addition of the probe. Following incubation, the reaction mixture was run on a 5% TBE native gel in 4 °C for 30 min to 1 h. The gel was subsequently imaged using a Bio-Rad ChemiDoc Gel Imager.

It has been revealed that the most effective gRNA sequence targeting an enhancer was cloned individually into the pBA904 vector and transfected into CRISPRi-HCASMC. After 5 days, RNA was collected, extracted and converted to cDNA. The effect of enhancer targeting was then assessed by comparing the expression levels of the target genes LOXL1, MYO9B, NAV1 and PALLD with that of the control. RNA was isolated using RNeasy plus micro kit (Qiagen, 74034) and total cDNA was prepared using High-capacity RNA-to-cDNA kit (Life Technologies, 4388950).

Industry observers note that parental and dCas9-Zim3 SMCs were cultured for 3 days in full medium (SmGM-2 Smooth Muscle Cell Growth Medium; Lonza, CC-3182) followed by 3 days serum starvation (base medium only) and 3 days recovery with full medium. dCas9-Zim3 SMCs were also cultured under two additional conditions for profiling: (1) 3 days full medium and (2) 3 days full medium followed by 3 days serum starvation. Cells were then processed using the Single Cell 3′ v.4 OCM kit (10x Genomics, PN-1000779) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The library was sequenced on an Illumina Nextseq2000 with read lengths (Read 1: 28, Read 2: 90, Index 1: 10, Index 2: 10). Sequencing data were demultiplexed and aligned to the human genome (GRCh38-2024-A from 10x Genomics) using CellRanger (v.9.0.1).

Industry observers note that library preparation was conducted with Chromium GEM-X Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits v.4 (10x Genomics). Libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq X Plus. The initial 10x scRNA-seq dataset was processed using the CellRanger pipeline (v.8.0.0). The workflow included demultiplexing the bcl files with CellRanger mkfastq, followed by running CellRanger count using the pre-built CellRanger reference GRCh38-2020-A from 10x Genomics.

Recent findings suggest that lentivirus carrying gRNAs were produced by VectorBuilder by modifying a CROPseq vector to include a T7–U6 hybrid promoter as described previously82. Four guides were designed per TSS, three guides per enhancer region and two non-targeting controls. gRNA lentiviruses were pooled for each enhancer or TSS at a 1:1 ratio based on titre for knockdown. Cells were transfected at a multiplicity of infection of 5 and left to recover for 3 days. Puromycin (0.5 μg ml−1) was used to select for transfected cells for 4 days. Cells then underwent the 3-day starvation and 3-day recovery period as described above during which growth was monitored in an Incucyte S3 incubator and images analysed using Incucyte 2020B software. Cells were then used for single-cell transcriptomic analysis as described below.

According to recent reports, A total of 100,000 cells from each condition were fixed with the Low Input Cell Fixation v.3 kit (Parse Biosciences, ECLC3303) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were processed with the Evercode WT v.3 kit (Parse Biosciences, ECWT3300). Eight sub-libraries of 12,500 cells were generated according to manufacturer’s instructions and sequenced on an Illumina Nextseq2000 with read lengths (Read 1, 64; Read 2, 58; Index 1: 8; Index 2, 8). Sequencing data were demultiplexed and aligned to the human genome (GRCh38 Parse Biosciences) using split-pipe (v.1.6.3).

Raw count matrices generated by Parse Biosciences split-pipe demultiplexing were imported into R using the ReadMtx function from Seurat v.4, loading the count matrix, cell metadata and gene annotation files from the DGE_filtered directory. A Seurat object was created requiring genes detected in at least three cells and a minimum of 200 features per cell. Mitochondrial content was calculated using PercentageFeatureSet. Cells were filtered to retain those with 200–7,500 detected genes and less than 25% mitochondrial reads. Untransduced cells and two genomic coordinate-labelled perturbation conditions were excluded. Perturbation identities were mapped from sample barcodes to gene or enhancer labels, and cells were classified as non-targeting or perturbed. Gene-expression data were normalized using Seurat NormalizeData, variable features identified with FindVariableFeatures and expression values scaled with ScaleData. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the RNA assay, followed by UMAP embedding using the top 30 principal components.

Industry observers note that local perturbation signatures were calculated using CalcPerturbSig from Seurat, subtracting the average expression of the k = 20 nearest non-targeting neighbour cells in PCA space (30 dimensions) to remove technical variation, producing a perturbation assay. The perturbation assay was centred, projected into PCA space using variable features from the RNA assay and visualized by UMAP. Mixscape83 was run on the scaled perturbation assay using RunMixscape with a minimum of five differentially expressed genes, ten iterations and perturbation type set to knockdown. This classified cells as knockdown, escaped or non-targeting based on posterior probability of perturbation. Escaped cells were excluded from all downstream analyses. Knockdown classification rates were computed per perturbation as the proportion of cells assigned knockdown status. Linkage disequilibrium analysis was performed on knockdown and non-targeting control cells using MixscapeLDA on the PRTB assay (ten principal components, log2[fold change] threshold 0.25) and a UMAP was computed on the top linear discriminant analysis dimensions for visualization of perturbation-specific clustering.

Differential expression between KD and non-targeting control cells was performed per perturbation using DESeq2 (v.1.52.0). Cells were assigned randomly to three pseudo-replicates within each perturbation and non-targeting control group, and raw counts were aggregated. Genes with fewer than ten total counts across pseudo-replicates were excluded. Differential expression was tested using a negative binomial model with perturbation condition as the independent variable. Results were filtered at FDR < 0.05.

Recent findings suggest that pre-ranked GSEA was performed per perturbation using fgsea (v.1.38.0) with genes ranked by log2[fold change] from DESeq2. Gene sets from MSigDB Hallmark and Gene Ontology Biological Process collections were obtained using the msigdbr (v.26.1.1) package (Homo sapiens). Minimum and maximum gene set sizes were set to 10 and 500, respectively, with 1,000 permutations. P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method across perturbations.

It has been revealed that pairwise cosine similarity was computed between the log2[fold change] vectors of all perturbations across the union of tested genes. Missing values were replaced with zero. Perturbations were clustered hierarchically on the resulting similarity matrix and visualized as a heatmap using pheatmap (v.1.0.13).

cNMF26,84 was applied to the raw count matrix of Mixscape-classified knockdown and non-targeting control cells. Counts were exported as an AnnData h5ad file and processed using the cNMF Python package (v.1.7.1). Genes expressed in fewer than five cells and all-zero genes were removed before factorization. Factorization was performed over k = 5–10 components with 100 iterations per k value and random seed 42. The optimal k = 8 was selected based on stability and reconstruction error, with a local-density threshold of 0.01 applied during consensus clustering; 99 of 800 (12%) outlier spectra were removed. Six of eight programmes were retained based on coherent gene set enrichment; two programmes dominated by unannotated loci and lacking enrichment were excluded. cNMF usage scores were imported back into R and added to the Seurat object metadata. Programme identity was assigned by over-representation analysis of the top 100 programme-specific genes against MSigDB Hallmark and Gene Ontology Biological Process gene sets using enricher from clusterProfiler (v.4.20.0).

In a recent development, transcription factor motif enrichment per cNMF programme was assessed by over-representation analysis of top 100 programme genes against Gene Transcription Regulation Database transcription factor target-gene sets from MSigDB C3. Transcription factor activity was estimated using the univariate linear model method implemented in decoupleR (v.2.17.0), with the DoRothEA regulon85 (confidence levels A–C) as the prior network. cNMF gene specificity score vectors (genes × programmes) were used as input. Transcription factors with the highest variance across programmes were retained for visualization.

FMC module scores were computed using AddModuleScore in Seurat on a curated list of FMC marker genes as described above. Stimulated SMC up- and down-regulated gene sets were derived from FindAllMarkers differential expression between stimulated (Zim3_3d3d) and control (Zim3_ctrl) conditions, filtered at FDR < 0.05 and |log2[fold change]| > 0.25. A signed stimulation score was computed as the difference between up- and down-regulated module scores. Spearman correlations between module scores and cNMF programme usage were computed using cor.test. Per perturbation mean scores were compared using the Wilcoxon rank sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The Spearman correlation between each perturbation’s full log2[fold change] profile and the signed stimulated SMC log2[fold change] vector was computed across shared genes.

Industry observers note that RRA86 was applied across all perturbation DESeq2 gene rankings using the RobustRankAggreg (v.1.2.1) R package, separately for upregulated and down-regulated genes ranked by adjusted P value. Genes passing FDR < 0.05 after Benjamini–Hochberg correction of RRA scores were retained as the convergent programme. Each gene was assigned a direction based on the RRA result with the lower score. The top 30 convergent genes by number of perturbations in which they reached significance were selected for visualization. A convergent programme score was computed per cell as the difference between up and down module scores using AddModuleScore. Pathway enrichment of convergent up and down-regulated genes was performed using enricher against MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets.

In a recent development, bulk in situ Hi-C libraries for 15 different coronary artery samples across a multi-ethnic cohort were generated with the Arima Hi-C kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Specifically, one Hi-C library was created from each biological sample, with an input of approximately 800,000 cells each. Restriction enzymes cutting at ^GATC and G^ANTC were used in library construction, and approximately 600 million reads were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 4000 per library.

Sources indicate that hi-C reads were processed with the nf-core Hi-C pipeline (v.2.0.0)87 and downstream maps were analysed at 5-kb resolution. Resolution assessment, library quality metrics, loop-caller benchmarking, inherent normalization and visualization procedures88,89 are described in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. Phased contact matrices using sample-specific genotypes were processed using Axiotl’s Turnkey platform (tinker.axiotl.com), which leverages Hi-C-Pro v.3.1.0 and cloud compute.

Industry observers note that we called cohort-specific 3D structures using the AQuA Tools framework90 for 3D genomics. Sample-wise chromatin structures were called in BEDPE format using extract_bedpe. We used union_bedpe to stack and merge BEDPE coordinates coming from various samples into one BEDPE file that contained the union set coordinates of all possible Hi-C connections in the cohort. This allowed for resolving overlapping interactions and outputting a common scaffold. To assign membership (as unique identifiers to column 7) to the stacked loops based on shared overlap of BEDPE anchors, we used cluster_bedpe. This resulting file became the mosaic for the cohort. To assess their functional and disease relevance, we intersected two-dimensional mosaic coordinates with one-dimensional genomic features including genes and snATAC peaks harbouring CAD GWAS variants. Against the mosaic BEDPE, contact values for each sample were queried in inherent and counts per million (CPM) numeric spaces using query_bedpe. All downstream analyses were performed in R.

It has been revealed that all experiments were performed on primary HCASMC between passages 4 and 7. Antibodies used for ChIP–qPCR were all pre-validated according to ChIP–seq guidelines. Purified rabbit monoclonal antibody against human CTCF (Abcam, ab128873; clone EPR7314(B)). Cell lines with various genotypes of rs4887091 were used. Approximately 2 × 106 HCASMC for each line were fixed with 1% formaldehyde and quenched by glycine. The cells were washed three times with PBS and then harvested in ChIP lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8, 5 mM EDTA, 0.5% SDS). Crosslinked chromatin was sheared for 2 × 1 min by sonication (Branson SFX250 Sonifier) before extensive centrifugation. Four volumes of ChIP dilution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100) was added to the supernatant. The resulting lysate was then incubated with Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo Scientific, 10009D) and antibodies at 4 °C overnight. Beads were washed once with buffer 1 (20 mM Tris pH 8, 2 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), once with buffer 2 (10 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), once with buffer 3 (10 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 250 mM LiCl, 1% NP40, 1% sodium deoxycholate monohydrate) and twice with TE buffer. DNA was eluted by ChIP elution buffer (0.1 M NaHCO3, 1% SDS, 20 μg ml−1 proteinase K). The elution was incubated at 65 °C overnight, and DNA was extracted with a DNA purification kit (Zymo, D4013). The purified DNA from various lines were analysed by qPCR using the ABI ViiA 7, with the same primer applied to each SNP. Assays were repeated at least three times. Data are average values ± s.d. of representative experiments.

CAD-associated variants were represented as 1-bp genomic intervals (hg38) and intersected with HCASMC CTCF ChIP–seq peak intervals. Observed overlap was defined as the number of CAD variants overlapping at least one CTCF peak. To estimate overlap expected by chance while preserving genomic structure, we performed chromosome-wise circular permutation of CTCF peak coordinates. For each chromosome, peak start coordinates were shifted by a random offset uniformly sampled from \([1,L-1]\), where L is chromosome length, with wraparound at chromosome boundaries. Peak widths and chromosome assignments were preserved. For each of B = 1,000 permutations, we recalculated the number of CAD variants overlapping permuted CTCF peaks to generate an empirical null distribution.

Fold enrichment was calculated as.

Empirical one-sided P values were computed as.

For parametric approximation, we set \({p}_{0}\) to the null mean overlap probability (mean(null overlaps)/N) and computed the exact one-sided binomial probability of observing \(\ge \)k overlaps among N variants.

In a recent development, enriched and input DNA were quantified by SYBR Green qPCR on ViiA 7. In addition to SYBR Green primers, we also used TaqMan genotyping probe (ThermoFisher, AN7EEGX, lot no. P260615-009) to directly amplify the different alleles of the DNA in heterozygous lines. Relative CTCF enrichment for target (rs4887091) and control loci was calculated as percent input. Target allele-specific binding effects were confirmed by benchmarking enrichment profiles against the expected quantitative gradients of the in-house validated allelic controls.

Sources indicate that to identify endogenous allelic controls across the four cell lines, CTCF ChIP–seq peaks were intersected with corresponding whole-genome sequencing VCF files. SNPs exhibiting complete genotypic gradients (homozygous reference, heterozygous, homozygous alternative) were scored for CTCF motif perturbation using the JASPAR matrix (MA0139.2). Allelic positive controls were defined by severe motif disruption (\(\Delta \text{Score}\ge 6.0\), max score \( > 8.0\)), whereas negative controls exhibited preserved motif integrity (\(\Delta \text{Score}\le 0.2\), both scores \( > 8.0\)).

It has been revealed that to prevent cross-cell-line amplification bias, SYBR Green qPCR primers (75–150 bp amplicons) were designed using Primer3 v.2.6.1. An in silico masking pipeline strictly discarded any candidate primer pairs whose binding sites overlapped with endogenous variants in the merged four-cell-line VCF, ensuring 100% conserved annealing kinetics across all biological samples.

According to recent reports, hi-ChIP was adapted from previously published protocols with some modifications91,92. Briefly, at least 1 million healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) and healthy HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde. The initial Hi-C portion followed the Arima Hi-C protocol described in the Arima High Coverage Hi-C Kit (Arima Genomics, A410110). For the immunoprecipitation step, sheared chromatin after the Hi-C portion of the protocol was immunoprecipitated with 5 μg of H3K27ac antibody (Abcam, ab4729) with 50 μl of protein G Dynabeads (Invitrogen 10004D) and allowed to incubate overnight at 4 °C. The protein G Dynabeads were washed and the immunoprecipitated DNA was de-crosslinked at 67 °C for 2 h and eluted (50 mM sodium bicarbonate, 1% SDS). Subsequently, Dynabeads MyOne Streptavidin C1 beads (Invitrogen, 65002) were used to enrich ligated junctions as per Hi-C protocol. Library preparation was performed using the NEB Ultra II library preparation kit (NEB, E7645L), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Twelve PCR cycles were performed using indexed primers and subsequently DNA fragments between 300 bp and 500 bp were size selected using the Omega MagBind NGS clean up Magnetic beads (Omega, M1378). The libraries were sequenced by paired-end sequencing with at least 300 million read pairs at 2 × 151-bp read length on Illumina HiSeq 4000 platforms. Raw paired-end reads in Fastq format for respective samples were processed using the Hi-CuP pipeline93 (v.0.7.4). The hg38 human genome was used as reference to generate the Hi-CuP Digest file using two restriction motifs GATC and GANTC using the hicup_digester command for running the Hi-CuP pipeline. Paired contacts were extracted from aligned filtered bam files using Samtools (v.1.13) and used as input for the pre function in the Juicer package to generate hic files94. Paired interaction counts at 5 kb resolution were extracted from the matrix, and high-confidence chromatin loops were identified using the FitHiChIP tool (v.11.0) as described previously using default parameters95. Using HCASMC and HCAEC ChIP–seq peak files as input, and initial paired interaction files, high-confidence peak-to-all interactions with a 5-kb bin size were processed using the bash FitHiChIP_HiCPro.sh script (https://ay-lab.github.io/FitHiChIP/). High-confidence chromatin interactions were sorted and indexed in bed format and converted to long-range format for visualization on the WashU browser. The overlay of Hi-ChIP, ChIP–seq and GWAS data was plotted using the locuszoomr package (v.0.3.5) and R (v.4.3.1).

ChIP–seq was performed as described previously with minor optimizations96. Briefly, 1 million HCASMCs and HCAECs from the same lot used for Hi-ChIP experiments were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature and quenched with glycine (125 mM) for 5 min. The cells were rinsed twice with cold 1× PBS and sonicated in nuclei lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES–KOH, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, 1% SDS, Takara, 1× protease inhibitor) using the Bioruptor sonicator to obtain chromatin fragments between 200 bp and 500 bp. The fragmented chromatin was immunoprecipitated overnight at 4 °C, with 5 μg of H3K27ac antibody (Abcam, ab4729) and 50 μl of protein G beads (Invitrogen, 10004D). Subsequently, the beads were washed and immunoprecipitated DNA was de-crosslinked and eluted in elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, and 10 mM EDTA). Eluted ChIP fragments were isolated using phenol–chloroform extraction method, and DNA was purified by ethanol precipitation. Library preparation was performed on the eluted ChIP DNA using the NEB Ultra II library preparation kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Ten PCR cycles were performed using indexed primers and the library of DNA fragments with sizes between 300 bp and 500 bp was selected using the Omega MagBind NGS clean up Magnetic beads (Omega, M1378). The libraries were sent for paired-end sequencing, with at least 50 million read pairs at 2 × 151-bp read length on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform. Paired-end sequencing reads were aligned to human genome (hg38) using BWA mem v.0.7.5 (ref. 97), and reads were deduplicated using Picard v.3.4.0 MarkDuplicates. Aligned mapped reads in BAM file were used as input for peak-calling using Dfilter98 to identify significant H3K27ac peaks using the following setting: -ks = 60, -bs = 100, -Ipvalue = 8. Bigwig tracks were normalized for sequencing depths and the sum of normalized binned tag-count represents the peak height.

Healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) were cultured in human vascular smooth muscle basal medium (Gibco, M231500), in Smooth Muscle Growth Supplement (Gibco, S00725) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Healthy HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were cultured in Endothelial Cell Growth medium MV2 (PromoCell, C-22022).

The Lentiguide-Puro plasmid was obtained as a gift from F. Zhang (Addgene, 52963, LentiGuide-Puro) in which the non-targeting control sgRNAs and sgRNAs targeting the TSS and regulatory enhancer were annealed and ligated into the Esp3I cut-site of the Lentiguide-Puro vector using T4 Ligase (NEB, M0202) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Ligation products were transformed into One Shot Stbl3 Chemically competent Escherichia coli (Invitrogen, C737303) and plasmids of positive clones were isolated using FavorPrep Plasmid DNA Extract Kit (Favorgen, FAPDE001-1). The CRISPR interference expression vector for Lenti-dCas9-KRAB-blast (Addgene, 89567) was a gift from G. Hon. For lentivirus production, HEK293T cells were cultured in DMEM + 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) until 70% confluency before transfection. Then, 10 μg of individual plasmids, 7.5 μg of pMDLg/RRE, 2.5 μg of pRSV-Rev and 2.5 μg of pMD2.G lentivirus packaging plasmids were co-transfected with 50 μl of polyethylenimine diluted in 3 ml of Opti-MEM I Reduced Serum Medium (ThermoFisher Scientific, 31985070). Medium was refreshed overnight with reduced 5% FBS in DMEM medium, and the expended medium was collected twice after 24 h and 48 h, respectively. Pooled supernatant was filtered through a polyethersulfone 0.45 μm filter and viral particles were concentrated using Viro-PEG Lentivirus Concentrator (Ozbiosciences, LVG100) as per the manufacturer’s instructions.

Cell kinetic proliferation live-cell imaging was performed using the HoloMonitor M4 system (Phase Holographic Imaging, PHI AB) using the Cell Kinetic Proliferation assay protocol as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Non-targeting controls and AMOTL2 dCas9-KRAB CRISPRi knockdown HCASMCs were seeded and cultured in vascular smooth muscle cell medium, in smooth muscle growth supplement, at a confluence of 15,000 cells cm−2 in a 24-well vessel (VWR, 734-2325) (n = 8). The 24-well HoloLid (PHI AB, 71130) was used to enhance the visualization and tracking of cells. At least five capture areas were taken per well, and time-lapse imaging at every 30-min time interval was taken across wells over 72 h. Cellular segmentation was performed using the HoloMonitor App Suite (v.3.5.2.446). Cellular confluence was captured and normalized to baseline at 0 h.

According to recent reports, total RNA was extracted using Trizol Reagent (ThermoFisher, 15596026) and Direct-Zol RNA miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, R2050). At least three independent replicates were used for RNA library preparations. RNA quality and yield was assessed using Agilent RNA 6000 pico kit (Agilent, 5067-1513) for quality. Bulk RNA-seq library preparations were prepared using VAHTS Universal V10 RNA-seq Library Prep Kit for Illumina (Vazyme, NR606-01) with Ribodepletion, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA libraries were prepared using Illumina RNA Truseq indexes and quantified using Agilent Tapestation. Sequencing was performed on the NovaSeq X Plus (PE150) by NovogeneAIT Singapore, yielding 50 million raw pair-end reads. Raw Fastq files were trimmed using the trim-galore tool (v.0.65) from Babraham Bioinformatics to sequence length of 50. Paired-end reads were mapped and aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38–hg38 using STAR aligner (v.2.7.0) as per default settings and using gene annotations from GENCODE v.38. Aligned gene counts were mapped using HTSeq-count v.2.1.2 and normalized to TPM by sequencing depth and by gene length. Differential gene-expression analysis was performed using EdgeR (v.3.42.4). Contrasts were compared between non-targeting control and AMOTL2 TSS knockdown cells. A negative binomial generalized log-linear model was used to model gene counts using the glmFit function. |log[fold change]| >0.5 and FDR < 0.05 cut-offs were used to identify significantly differentially expressed genes following multiple testing correction. Figures were generated with R v.3.5.1.

HCASMCs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (ThermoFisher, 5090495) for 15 min at room temperature, then washed with 3× PBS for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were permeabilized with PBS with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 min, followed by blocking in 5% normal goat serum in PBS (blocking buffer) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary anti-Calponin (1:100) (ProteinTech, 13938-1-AP), and primary anti-α-smooth muscle actin antibody (1:100) (Sigma-Aldrich, A5228) were diluted in blocking buffer and added to permeabilized cells overnight at 4 °C. After washing with PBS three times for 5 min, cells were incubated with Alexa fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:1,000) (Goat anti-mouse 594, ThermoFisher, A-11032; goat anti-rabbit 488, ThermoFisher, A-11008) and 1 μg ml−1 DAPI for 1 h at room temperature. Stained cells were washed three times for 5 min each with PBS, and images were acquired under the same laser exposure and magnification using a fluorescence microscope (EVOS M7000).

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Raw and processed sequencing files can be found as follows: Human Coronary Multi-ome: GSE328800. Human Coronary Hi-C: GSE328970. Genotyping for Human Samples: dbGaP accession ID phs004118.v1.p1. HCASMC Perturb–seq: GSE347104. CTCF ChIP–seq in HCASMCs: GSE319778. H3K27ac/Hi-ChIP in HCASMC and HCAEC: GSE282556 and GSE282557. Bulk RNA-seq AMOTL2: GSE329169. Public and/or reference resources used in this study include GTEx v.8, the 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 reference panel and the GRCh38–hg38 human reference genome. Previously published datasets used for validation or reference mapping include GSE131780, GSE175621 and GSE188422.

Scripts used for analysis in this manuscript can be found at GitHub (https://github.com/jamrute/CAD-scV2E2G).

#153107. Chelsea Transfer News: Alonso Tells Right-Back To Leave

Chelsea Transfer News: Alonso Tells Right-Back To Leave

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (401 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Footballtransfertavern

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chelsea transfer news: Xabi Alonso has reportedly told Malo Gusto to find a new club, according to CaughtOffside, who are citing Simon Phillips’ Substack.
  • They tried to sign Gusto on loan on deadline day, but Chelsea refused anything short of a permanent deal.
  • Sources indicate that gusto’s standing has slipped quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea transfer news: Xabi Alonso has reportedly told Malo Gusto to find a new club, according to CaughtOffside, who are citing Simon Phillips’ Substack. The report claims the 23-year-old France international does not suit the wing-back system Alonso has built at Stamford Bridge. It also floats a surprise swap that would send Gusto to Liverpool and reunite Alonso with Jeremie Frimpong, his former Bayer Leverkusen right wing-back.

Liverpool’s interest has history. They tried to sign Gusto on loan on deadline day, but Chelsea refused anything short of a permanent deal. Their right-back problem has run since Trent Alexander-Arnold left. Frimpong cost around £29.5million and has battled injuries and form, while Ronald Araujo is a centre-back covering on a season-long loan from Barcelona.

Sources indicate that gusto’s standing has slipped quickly. He started three of the first four league games, yet Josh Acheampong has since taken his place, and reports say he will be fourth choice behind Acheampong, Marco Palestra and Reece James once James returns from injury in early 2027.

It has been revealed that his strength is defending, with 73 tackles and 36 chances created in 45 appearances last season. The weakness is end product, because three goals and five assists are modest for a wing-back who must supply Alonso’s right-hand width.

Industry observers note that frimpong supplies exactly that. The 25-year-old Dutchman scored 28 of his 30 Leverkusen goals under Alonso and thrives on pace and early crosses. Defending is his flaw, at 5ft 8in and with a poor injury record at Anfield.

In a recent development, no. Chelsea are fifth with 16 points from 10 games, but they have lost four, including 1-0 at Sunderland last Sunday and 3-0 at Brentford, and they concede too easily. Frimpong would add another attacker to a right side that already has James, Acheampong, Palestra and Pedro Neto, and he does nothing for a shaky back line. With no European football this season, Chelsea don’t need that many right-sided options anyway.

The money matters too. Both players have contracts until 2030 and similar valuations, so a straight swap brings Chelsea no cash and leaves Liverpool with their problem solved.

Sell Gusto instead, preferably abroad, since Paris Saint-Germain have been linked and Chelsea are reportedly open to cutting their asking price. Then spend that fee on a defensive midfielder or centre-back, because that is where Alonso’s team needs help.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.
  • Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others.
  • Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the problems Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Industry observers note that thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N.

Recent findings suggest that the last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

According to recent reports, “We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”.

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

Industry observers note that what they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

According to recent reports, james Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU.

Sources indicate that the roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Industry observers note that hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI.

It must be remarked the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

The whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

Valencia will aim to post a third straight win in all competitions when they continue their La Liga campaign at home to Osasuna on Sunday afternoon.

Los Che comfortably lead the overall head-to-head record between the two sides, having posted 46 wins to Osasuna's 21, while 25 of their 92 matches have finished all square.

Valencia boast a record of three wins, three draws and seven defeats from their 13 league matches this season, with 12 points leaving them in 17th spot in the La Liga table.

It has been a tricky first third of the league season for Valencia, but there have been signs of life in recent weeks, having won two of their last three in the league and three of their last four in all competitions.

Javier Aguirre's side will enter this match off the back of a 1-0 win over Rayo Vallecano in La Liga, while they also beat Tavernes 6-0 in the Copa del Rey on November 10.

Valencia, who finished ninth in Spain's top flight last season, actually have the second-worst home record in La Liga this season, securing only two points from seven league games in front of their own supporters.

Los Che are also the joint-second lowest goalscorers in La Liga this term with nine, and that is a concerning record heading towards the winter break in Spain's top flight.

As for Osasuna, a record of four wins, three draws and six defeats from 13 matches has brought them 15 points, which is enough for 13th spot at this stage of proceedings.

Jagoba Arrasate's side will enter this match off the back of a 1-0 win over Malaga, but they did lose their last away fixture - a 2-1 reverse to Deportivo La Coruna on November 2.

Los Rojillos have struggled on their travels this season, claiming only three points from six matches, suffering five defeats in the process.

Osasuna lost 1-0 to Valencia in the corresponding match during the 2025-26 campaign, and they have only managed to win one of the last five games between the two sides.

That said, Osasuna do have a recent away success against Valencia to their name, having recorded a 2-1 victory at Mestalla in August 2023.

Valencia will welcome Jose Gaya back into their squad this weekend following a suspension, but Sergi Canos, Diego Lopez and Jesus Vazquez are again expected to miss the contest.

Arnaut Danjuma is likely to return to the squad, with the attacker not involved against Rayo Vallecano last time out following the death of his father.

Gaya for Pablo Maffeo could be the only change from the team's last match given the impressive nature of both the performance and the result.

As for Osasuna, Alejandro Catena is out of the game through suspension, with the 32-year-old sent off in the team's home success over Malaga last time out.

Jorge Herrando was back on the bench against Malaga after recovering from an injury and could now be introduced into the starting team here.

Ante Budimir has scored nine times in 13 league appearances this season, and the Croatian will once again lead the Osasuna line in this contest.

However, Abel Bretones, Aitor Fernandez and Rockson Yeboah are still injured.

Osasuna possible starting lineup:.

A stalemate could be on the cards at Mestalla.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea have all contacted Bournemouth about England midfielder Alex Scott, according to CaughtOffside, which cites The i Paper.
  • According to recent reports, the interest has clear reasons behind it.
  • Scott wins the ball, presses and carries it through midfield, and he started Bournemouth’s first five league games this season before a quadriceps injury on England duty in October kept him out for weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea have all contacted Bournemouth about England midfielder Alex Scott, according to CaughtOffside, which cites The i Paper. Liverpool and Chelsea want to move in January, while Arsenal would rather wait until next summer. Bournemouth’s stance on selling the 23-year-old has softened, but the reported asking price is above £100m, and Scott turned down two contract offers over the summer.

According to recent reports, the interest has clear reasons behind it. Andoni Iraola coached Scott at Bournemouth before taking over at Anfield in June, and Liverpool want to reunite them. Chelsea lost Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City in a £125m deadline-day deal and had a reported £64m bid for Scott rejected earlier in the summer. Arsenal already have Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Zubimendi and Myles Lewis-Skelly, so CaughtOffside sees Chelsea or Liverpool as the more logical destinations for his playing time.

Scott wins the ball, presses and carries it through midfield, and he started Bournemouth’s first five league games this season before a quadriceps injury on England duty in October kept him out for weeks. Fitness is the first concern, because knee problems have interrupted much of his time on the south coast. End product is the second. He has scored five league goals in 85 appearances since joining in 2023, so he will not solve a shortage of chances alone.

Not at £100m, and not as a January priority. Liverpool rank 18th for substantial chances after ten league games, according to This Is Anfield, and Scott offers energy rather than creativity. The real gap sits beside Ryan Gravenberch, where Curtis Jones left in the summer, and nobody arrived to share the defensive work.

Scott could be the aggressive partner in Iraola’s double pivot, freeing Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz to play higher, yet that is a heavy fee for a player only just rebuilding match fitness, with Liverpool fourth and nine points behind Arsenal.

Recent findings suggest that chelsea’s case is simpler. The division’s biggest summer spenders lost their midfield engine and can justify the price more easily. Arsenal’s patience makes sense, since Rice, Guimaraes and Zubimendi leave no room for a £100m squad player. A Liverpool bid would only inflate the market Chelsea are already shaping. If Iraola wants a January signing, a specialist holding midfielder for far less money does more for the top-four push.

By Matt Law | 27 Nov 2026 10:13, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 10:16.

Two teams enjoying solid campaigns in Spain's top flight thus far will lock horns on Sunday evening, as Real Sociedad welcome Sevilla to Anoeta Stadium.

Real Sociedad just about lead the overall head-to-head record between the two sides, having posted 55 victories to Sevilla's 52, while 35 of their 142 fixtures have finished level.

Real Sociedad will enter this weekend's match off the back of a 2-1 defeat to Crystal Palace in the Europa League, with the result leaving them down in 27th spot in the overall table and out of the knockout round playoffs at this stage of proceedings.

It has been a struggle for Real Sociedad in Europe this season, and they were also beaten 3-2 by Racing de Santander in Spain's top flight last weekend, so the Basque team will be bidding to avoid a third straight loss in all competitions on Sunday night.

La Real have had a strong campaign in Spain's top flight, with a record of seven wins, one draw and five defeats from 13 matches bringing them 22 points, which is enough for fifth spot in the La Liga table.

Pellegrino Matarazzo's side now have three straight league games against Sevilla, Real Madrid and Villarreal before returning to European action at home to Torreense on December 10.

Real Sociedad have been strong at home in the league this season, boasting a record of four wins, one draw and one defeat, picking up 13 points from six matches.

Sevilla have won five, drawn four and lost four of their 13 league matches this season, with 19 points leaving them in sixth spot in the table, three points behind fifth-placed Real Sociedad.

The Red and Whites are without a win in their last three La Liga fixtures, though, losing at Getafe at the start of the month before drawing back-to-back games with Alaves and Real Betis.

Luis Garcia Plaza's side have only actually won one of their last seven league matches, but sitting sixth after 13 games represents a solid start to the campaign.

Sevilla recorded a 1-0 win over Real Sociedad when the two teams last locked horns in May 2026, but the corresponding game last season ended in a 2-1 success for the Basque outfit.

Los Nervionenses have picked up eight points from their six away league matches during the 2026-27 campaign courtesy of a record of two wins, two draws and two defeats.

Head coach Matarazzo will make changes to the side that started against Palace in the Europa League, with Carlos Soler, Orri Oskarsson, Igor Zubeldia, Sergio Gomez and Luka Sucic among those set to return to the team for this match.

Mikel Oyarzabal has only scored three times this season, but the Spain international will continue in the final third of the field for the Basque outfit.

Sevilla will once again be without the services of Marcao, Jose Angel Carmona, Alfon Gonzalez and Miguel Sierra on Sunday due to injury problems.
