  • NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft rolled out almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft rolled out almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

Recent findings suggest that when Voyager 1 rolled out, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

In a recent development, that's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," notes Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

In a recent development, the spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

Recent findings suggest that but if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eleven rounds into the Serie A season, Juventus have neither won nor conceded a penalty, a distinction shared only with Torino. With the league's penalty rate down and the team seventh, the João Mario handball in Florence has become the clearest example of a call that went against them.

Industry observers note that juventus have reached the November break without a single penalty decision in their league matches. Seven sides are still waiting for a penalty in their favour: Roma, Juventus, Torino, Lecce, Fiorentina, Sassuolo and Udinese. Seven have yet to concede one: Inter, Milan, Como, Juventus, Napoli, Torino and Genoa. Only the two Turin clubs appear on both lists.

That makes Juventus an outlier, even in a season of fewer spot-kicks. Sportmediaset puts the number of teams still waiting for a penalty partly down to the new refereeing approach introduced by Orsato.

According to recent reports, the wider numbers show a quieter season from the spot. The 24 penalties so far work out at about 0.22 per match, compared with 0.28 and 0.27 in the two previous seasons. The drop was sharpest early on. Only five of the 24 penalties came in the first five rounds.

Sources indicate that the trend has not been flat since then. The rate rose to 0.31 per match after the September international break. Juventus have not shared in that rise. Their total in both columns remains zero.

Sources indicate that the contrast with last season is clear. Juventus were awarded five league penalties then. They also had the last three saved: David’s against Lecce, Yildiz’s against Cremonese and Locatelli’s against Sassuolo.

The case that has drawn most attention came late in the 2-2 draw at Fiorentina. João Mario handled the ball. No penalty was given. Gianluca Rocchi, who now works as a DAZN pundit, noted it should have been a spot-kick. His reasoning was that the arm was out wide and the player had time to move it, even though the ball came from a teammate.

Luciano Spalletti signalled that he also saw a penalty. He chose not to complain publicly about the decision.

Close calls carry weight at this stage. Juventus are seventh on 18 points, six behind fourth place. Champions League qualification is in doubt. An injury-hit squad cannot easily absorb lost points from decisions at the margins.

It has been revealed that the run after the break will test whether the pattern holds. Venezia, the next league opponents, are among five clubs to have conceded three penalties, the league’s highest total. Frosinone, Bologna, Atalanta and Sassuolo share that figure. Sassuolo are also on the list of sides yet to be awarded one.

In a recent development, the schedule is crowded. After Venezia, Juventus host Omonia in the Europa League. A league trip to Como follows, then Sassuolo at home in the Coppa Italia. Como have yet to concede a penalty this season.

In a recent development, the first of those fixtures has already moved. Lega Serie A brought Juventus v Venezia forward to Sunday 22 November at 12:30, from its original slot on Monday 23 November at 20:45.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

It has been revealed that he was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo remarked the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed.".

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head stated of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

It has been revealed that he has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the initiative but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

Just eight universities dominate Nobel and other top economics prizes

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers from Harvard and seven other US universities including MIT, Princeton and Yale, dominate economics prizes.Credit: Jade Gao/AFP via Getty.
  • Major prizes in economics, including the Nobel are being awarded to researchers affiliated to an increasingly concentrated set of US universities, according to a working paper published last month1.
  • Eight institutions dominate the world's top economics prizes, led Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers from Harvard and seven other US universities including MIT, Princeton and Yale, dominate economics prizes.Credit: Jade Gao/AFP via Getty.

Major prizes in economics, including the Nobel are being awarded to researchers affiliated to an increasingly concentrated set of US universities, according to a working paper published last month1.

Eight institutions dominate the world's top economics prizes, led Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

In a recent development, this contrasts with prizes awarded in disciplines in the natural sciences, engineering and social sciences outside economics. These have become less concentrated among certain instituions over the past 70 years, according to the working paper, which has not yet been peer reviewed.

“The whole world now does science,” claims Richard Freeman, an economist at Harvard University and an author on the paper, which is an revision to an article presented at a National Bureau of Economic Research Summer Institute workshop in a 20242. “Our initial thought was that as the science spreads out, so too should all the prizes.” And that was the case — except in economics where “it went the other direction”.

Economist John Hassler, who is based at Stockholm University and chairs the prize-awarding committee for the Economics Prize in Memory of Alfred Nobel, notes that the overall finding of concentration among a small group of US universities is not a complete surprise.

According to recent reports, “The trend is truly eye-opening and adds another dimension to the understanding of inequality within the economics profession,” adds Ashwini Deshpande, an economist at Ashoka University in Sonipat, India. “The low levels of gender, ethnic and geographic diversity within authors of top journal papers and prizes is well known and a matter of concern.”.

Freeman and his colleagues examined 171 different awards and focused their analyses on those given between 1960 and 2022, including Nobel prizes (except for literature and peace), the Fields Medal for mathematics and the Breakthrough science prizes established in 2012 by the founders of technology companies among others.

The authors of the working paper analysed the academic affiliations of the 5,859 prizewinners, working out the number of years they were linked to a specific institution. They call this metric ‘affiliation years’.

Industry observers note that of the 18 scientific fields of the prizewinners, 17 had a greater variety of universities represented among recipients over the time period. Economics was the outlier.

In a recent development, among winners of the economics Nobel prize, seven out of 148 institutions made up 50% of affiliation years. It means that, of all the years that economics Nobel prizewinners dedicated to their discipline in academia, half of them were spent in the seven institutions.

For chemistry Nobels, 23 institutions out of 216 accounted for half of affiliation years. Twenty-six out of 243 institutions accounted for 50% of affiliation years for the physiology or medicine Nobel, and 17 out of 200 for the physics prize.

When the authors assessed all the main economics prizes between 1960 and 2022 (not only the Nobel), they found that researchers from eight out of 249 institutions represented 50% of affiliation years. In addition to Harvard, the eight are: the University of Chicago in Illinois; Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge; Stanford University in California; Princeton University in New Jersey; Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut; the University of California, Berkeley; and Columbia University in New York.

It has been revealed that by contrast, for assessed prizes in the natural sciences, 37 institutions out of 1,318 account for 50% of affiliation-years as of 2022; for engineering prizes it is 27 out of 783; and for social sciences prizes (minus economics), it is 23 out of 744. Unlike in economics, the trend for these fields is towards less concentration (see ‘Spot the outlier’).

The authors propose some possible explanations. One of these relates to another finding of the paper: “The institutions producing most of the field’s recognized work also establish the toolkit that the rest of the fields adopts,” the paper’s authors say. “Work using an unfamiliar approach is hard to place or recognize, and findings that disagree with the main tenets of the field are rejected rather than studied as special cases that may yield new knowledge.”.

Another factor, they report is that in economics, 55 per cent of Nobel laureates received the prize for a broad body of work. This contrasts somewhat with medicine and the other sciences. Some 50 per cent of prize winners in chemistry, 59 per cent in physics and 70 per cent in medicine were awarded for testable findings.

Hanzhang Zhou, a co-author on the paper and an economics doctoral candidate at MIT, states: “When you’re giving the prize for somebody’s lifetime agenda, the institution that they’re associated with is usually one of the factors that you do take into account,” she explains.

Hassler told Nature that the economics prize is not intended to be a lifetime achievement award and follows the rules governing the other prize categories. He claims it is a prize for a well-defined contribution or breakthrough, should also lead to further research in the field and that the finding must also have relevance to society at large.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03333-3.

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 04:00 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 06:54 EST, 26 November 2026.

Manchester United legend Peter Schmeichel fears Senne Lammens has yet to recover from the blunder he made during Belgium's World Cup campaign last summer.

Lammens made two costly mistakes in United’s 2-2 Champions League draw with Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday night, conceding a needless penalty and dropping a clanger in the dying minutes to allow Luis Suarez to score twice for the home side.

The 24-year-old goalkeeper, who was one of Manchester United's standout performers last season following his £18.1million transfer from Royal Antwerp, has looked unconvincing so far this term and played a part in the club conceding more goals (35) than any other side in Europe's top five leagues.

Former Red Devils goalkeeper Schmeichel believes Lammens has never fully recovered from his error that led to Belgium being dumped out by Spain at the World Cup quarter-final stage last summer.

In the 88th minute of the match, with the score locked at 1-1, Lammens spilled the ball into the path of Mikel Merino, who tapped home to send Spain through to the semi-finals.

Asked if the confidence-shot goalkeeper should now be dropped by Mauricio Pochettino for Karl Darlow, who was signed by United in the summer, Schmeichel told CBS Sports: ‘I don’t know where that point is.

Senne Lammens made two massive errors during Manchester United's 2-2 draw at Sporting Lisbon.

Peter Schmeichel fears Lammens has never fully recovered from his blunder at the World Cup.

‘Mauricio Pochettino has come in, he’s brought his own staff, that means he’s got a newly introduced goalkeeping coach and maybe that is something that can change it for him.

‘I don’t know if you remember in the World Cup, he came against Spain and made a bit of a mistake, Merino scored and they got knocked out, and I feel like he’s lost a little bit of confidence from that mistake, hasn’t really recovered.

‘As a goalkeeper when you’re not on your best form you need your defenders in front of you to help you out and the sad truth is that they haven’t been able to do that and of course, that makes it so much worse.'.

Joshua Zirkzee insists United’s players will rally around Lammens and won’t let their under-fire goalkeeper ‘suffer by himself’.

The two costly errors undid Lammens’ good work after he saved an earlier penalty from Suarez, but Zirkzee said the players are determined to support the Belgian.

‘This team is a family, so there's no one who will suffer by themselves,’ said Zirkzee. ‘Mistakes happen. Let's go on to the next one. Senne’s a great goalkeeper.

According to recent reports, ‘In this moment, we just give him space. I’m not sure if he wants to hear anything at all. But Senne’s a great kid. He's got a good head on him and we all know that next game he is going to be at the top of his game. We didn't draw because of him. I'm also someone who likes to look at myself and, you know, I didn't score.’.

United had two goals disallowed by Polish referee Szymon Marciniak as well as conceding the two penalties and seeing Youri Tielemans sent off – three days after Leny Yoro was shown a controversial red card at Liverpool – and Zirkzee admitted that it feels like the world is against Pochettino’s team at the moment.

The Belgian shot-stopper conceded a needless penalty just minutes after saving a spot-kick.

He then spilled the ball into the path of Luis Suarez late on, gifting Sporting a late equaliser.

Industry observers note that ‘Yeah, we're in a place where it can feel like that pretty quick,’ he added. ‘But as I said, we've got a locker-room that's built on supporting each other and we will get out of it eventually. If it's us against the world, so be it.

‘For the team that we are, we shouldn't really be looking at what the referee decides, but you cannot deny that it was some key decisions that weren't in our favour, to put it like that.

‘But, as I said, we shouldn't really be looking at the referee. All we have to do is look at ourselves. In the end, I think we drew because of small details, little mistakes. But we definitely have something to build on, mainly the way we started the second half. I think that's something we can build on and move on with. Our team should be capable to win even if we're not being favoured in those moments.’.

Separated by eight places in the Premier League table, 18th-placed Sunderland welcome mid-table Tottenham Hotspur to the Stadium of Light in matchweek 12.

The Black Cats have found greater defensive balance in recent weeks to sit inside the bottom three on goal difference alone, offering encouragement ahead of facing Roberto De Zerbi's men, who have won four of their last five matches.

Sunderland continue to struggle for victories this season, but the Wearside outfit's recent results suggest that Regis Le Bris intends to address their underwhelming start by strengthening their defensive foundations.

Le Bris's men collected four points at the start of the campaign before suffering four consecutive defeats, during which the Mackems conceded at least twice against Arsenal, Manchester City, Brighton & Hove Albion and Bournemouth.

Having failed to score in three of those four defeats, the Black Cats' problems at both ends of the pitch were laid bare.

Shutting out Leeds United, however, began a sequence in which Sunderland have kept three clean sheets in four matches, although their only Premier League victory during that period remains the 1-0 success over Chelsea at the start of the month.

Nonetheless, those shutouts suggest that Le Bris intends to repair his leaky defence before turning his attention to a misfiring attack.

That approach could prove useful when Spurs visit Wearside this weekend, with De Zerbi's men occasionally struggling against opponents content to surrender possession and frustrate them.

Sunderland's counter-attacking approach troubled Chelsea three weeks ago, and De Zerbi's men will hope to avoid the pitfalls that befell the Blues in that early-November encounter.

The North Londoners arrive buoyed by four victories in their last five matches, including three clean sheets, while the absence of European commitments has given them a full week to prepare.

That should benefit the 10th-placed visitors, although the joint-lowest scorers in the top half must deliver a strong away performance to climb the standings, with the capital club just three points behind fifth-placed Bournemouth.

Spurs could finish the weekend in the Europa League position currently occupied by the Cherries, although that would require Marco Rose's men to slip up and Brentford, Leeds, Chelsea and Everton all to fail to win.

Without joint-leading scorer Brobbey, the Black Cats will look to Enzo Le Fee to add to his three goals or another player to provide a match-winning contribution.

Although only Dominic Solanke and Jan Paul van Hecke have scored more than once for Spurs, the visitors can call upon Mohammed Kudus's creativity and ability to score from unlikely positions at the Stadium of Light.

Youngster Luca Jamie Williams-Barnett excelled on his full debut for the club, scoring and setting up Solanke's second-half strike to stake a strong claim for another start.

On the injury front, Xavi Simons (knee) and Wilson Odobert (knee) remain long-term absentees, while Mathys Tel (Achilles), Mykhailo Mudryk (ankle) and Savio (thigh) are unavailable in the short term; Tosin Adarabioyo (calf) faces fitness tests before Sunday, although Sandro Tonali is understood to have recovered from the illness that kept him out of last weekend's victory over Ipswich Town.

However, Brobbey's absence limits the hosts' attacking options, and the visitors' four victories in five mean we back them to edge a low-scoring contest.

Tech Report: Juventus sell out Venezia game as Omonia sales pass 35,000

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Juventus have sold out Sunday's Serie A home game against Venezia despite a long injury list.
  • Juventus go into Sunday’s home game against Venezia still short of players.
  • According to recent reports, general sale for the fixture opened at 3pm on Tuesday 6 October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Juventus have sold out Sunday's Serie A home game against Venezia despite a long injury list. Strong early sales for the Europa League visit of Omonia Nicosia keep the club in line for another strong European crowd.

Juventus go into Sunday’s home game against Venezia still short of players. Several remain unavailable for Sunday’s 12:30 kick-off. Edon Zhegrova has trained with the group and is considered available. Celik, Cambiaso, Nico Gonzalez and Kalulu remain out, Sport Mediaset reported. For Spalletti, a full home crowd arrives in the middle of a busy run of games.

According to recent reports, general sale for the fixture opened at 3pm on Tuesday 6 October. Supporters living in the province of Venezia could buy only if they held an active Juventus Card. The fixture belongs to the 2026-27 Serie A Enilive season.

It has been revealed that this season every Juventus match ticket is digital. Each one is managed through the Allianz Stadium App.

Sources indicate that season-ticket holders who cannot attend can list their seat on resale.juventus.com. The club, not the seller, sets the resale price. A few of those listings are now all that remains for supporters who missed the general sale, ANSA reported.

In a recent development, the season-ticket terms also reward turning up. To keep first refusal on a 2027-28 season ticket, a holder must use the seat for at least 70 per cent of matches. That means at least 13 of the 19 league games.

In a recent development, the Europa League has drawn big numbers to Turin this season. Against NEC, 39,308 match tickets were sold, with away fans counted separately. No away figure was released for the Rennes visit, but that section was full.

The Rennes game finished 2-2 on 22 October. Juventus needed a second-half Woltemade penalty to draw after trailing 2-1.

Recent findings suggest that omonia Nicosia are next. Bookings for the Cypriot club’s visit still trail the two earlier European crowds.

Sources indicate that juventus have set strict conditions for the fixture. Supporters of Cypriot nationality may buy tickets only for the away section. The club has warned that breaking UEFA rules can lead to cancelled tickets and refused entry.

Taken together, the figures are consistent with a home support that keeps buying despite the injury list. The weekend league fixture will be followed by a European night that is already well on its way to another large crowd.

Juventus host Omonia Nicosia in the Europa League on 26 November.

In a recent development, liverpool transfer news from Goal says Ajax teenager Abdellah Ouazane is a January target as attacking cover for Florian Wirtz. Julian Ward, Liverpool’s recruitment chief, has reportedly sped up plans to support the £116m playmaker, and Ouazane has become a serious option before the winter window opens. Wael Mohya and Gilberto Mora sit on the same shortlist.

The 17-year-old grew up supporting Liverpool and badly wants to play at Anfield. Ajax hold the leverage, though: his contract runs to 2028, and persuading them to sell a prized academy graduate mid-season will take careful negotiation. By Axel Clody | 27 Nov 2026 12:28.

In Brazil, Fluminense's youth academy is considered one of the best because of the number of players it has produced this century. And Xerem's greatest achievement was simultaneously having a generation of young players who reached the highest levels of world football.

It has been revealed that all born in 2001, Joao Pedro (Chelsea), Luiz Henrique (Zenit), Andre (Wolverhampton Wanderers) and Matheus Martinelli (still at Fluminense) shared what was called the 'Golden Generation' of Xerem. Evanilson (Bournemouth), who is older and was born in 1999, was also in the team with them at some point in the youth system.

Three players who play or have played in the Premier League. One who was at the last World Cup. And another who won the Copa Libertadores with Fluminense and is still a starter for the team. A very rare feat that, for Gustavo Leal, who coached this generation for four years, was no coincidence.

The coach, recently runner-up in the Canadian Premier League with Atletico Ottawa, spoke with Trivela last week and explained the secrets to such a decisive generation.

Leal progressed from the Under-13s to the Under-20s in Fluminense's youth system and led this special group for four years. From the privileged position he held in this process, he understands that it was no coincidence and that the club, through its training methodology, plays a significant role in the development of these athletes.

'I strongly believe in the process and I do not think it is a coincidence that so many good players are in the same generation. It was a combination of the individual quality of the athletes and the good professionals they worked with. Xerem has many good people in goalkeeper training, in the physical area and in psychology' - he stated.

The 40-year-old coach highlighted that several coaches had led them, such as Leonardo Ramos in the Under-13s (now in the Under-20s at Internacional), Thiago Macedo (who was Gustavo Leal's assistant in jobs in Mexico and Chile) and Marcelo Veiga, who right now coordinates the Xerem youth academy.

In a recent development, 'This generation went through many good coaches. And this, combined with the quality that these players already had, allowed us to have such a large number of top-level players in the same generation' - he added.

When asked by reporters who surprised him most in this golden generation, Leal immediately chose Joao Pedro.

He then pointed out that it was not necessarily a surprise, but that what the striker has achieved is impressive. The 25-year-old was voted Chelsea's best player by fans last season and is maintaining that form this season.

'We always saw that Joao Pedro had a different kind of quality. Ever since he arrived in the Under-13s, we could already tell he was a special player. I think that, however optimistic we are and however much we work with the players to help them reach their full potential, perhaps we cannot imagine that this potential will be realised so quickly and at such a high level' - he commented.

Juventus president Gianluca Ferrero set out the leadership's view of the rebuild at the Brussels launch of the club's European Union fan club. He spoke while a capital raise of about €200m is open and a UEFA settlement limits spending.

Juventus president Gianluca Ferrero went to Brussels on 18 November with a clear message for supporters. Restoring the club to its former self is its absolute ambition, he noted, adding that the club is following the path set out by its chief executive and is confident this can happen. He spoke at the opening of the Juventus Official Fan Club European Union, which is chaired by MEP Sandro Gozi. The timing gives the statement weight.

It has been revealed that the new supporters’ club opened at the Iosono il Piemonte event space. Its stated purpose is to link Juventus supporters with the institutional centre of Europe.

Before the opening, the delegation went to the European Parliament with Gozi. Chief Club Affairs Officer Giorgio Chiellini led the group alongside Ferrero. Piedmont regional president Alberto Cirio attended the opening, as did MEPs who have joined the fan club.

The visit showed Chiellini’s work on the club’s relations with institutions and European football. It also gives supporters an official club in Brussels.

Industry observers note that the financial backdrop is demanding. Juventus posted a consolidated loss of €66m for 2025/26. On 12 November, the board approved the offer, using part of the €250m authority granted by shareholders at the extraordinary meeting on 3 November.

The offer involves up to 208.5m new shares at €0.96 each. Shareholders can buy one new share for every two they hold. The price is 28.36% below the theoretical ex-rights price, based on that day’s share price. The remaining €50m of the authority can be used in later financial years, depending on the club’s financial needs and investment intends.

According to recent reports, the spending limits come from UEFA. European football’s governing body fined Juventus €20m for breaking the football earnings rule. Of that amount, €14m is conditional. The club agreed a three-year settlement with annual targets. It also faces limits on registering latest players on its UEFA List A.

Those are the limits within which Ferrero’s ambition must be pursued. Any improvement in the squad has to fit within the annual targets agreed with UEFA.

Subscription rights can be traded on Euronext Milan until 25 November, and the offer closes on 1 December 2026.

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war.".

The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing.".

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius mentioned.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Former US President Joe Biden's newly introduced autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts.".

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel.".

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she promptly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk remarked he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges.".

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights.".

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the looks would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

Recent findings suggest that france was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

Recent findings suggest that the Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC mentioned that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC mentioned in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, mentioned it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC noted it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

Industry observers note that the ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

Recent findings suggest that the ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger noted the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck.".

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp stated that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he mentioned.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support.".

In a statement issued after the announcement of the prepares, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it noted.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the aims, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he noted.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he remarked, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals.".

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The strategy to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius declared on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the newly introduced funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously revealed, as well as upcoming radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also mentioned that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has stated he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He remarked Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and fresh transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents.".

It also mentioned that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank.".

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 upcoming businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR remarked the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also noted that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Prepares announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the strategy, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law.".

Meanwhile, more latest businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

  • Aston Villa will be bidding to extend a 42-year streak when they face Ipswich Town on Saturday evening.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 27 Nov 2026 12:29.

Aston Villa will be bidding to extend a 42-year streak when they face Ipswich Town on Saturday evening.

Unai Emery's side make the trip to Portman Road sitting in the bottom half of the Premier League table.

Furthermore, Villa are right now on a six-match winless streak, leading to Sports Mole arguing that Emery is no longer untouchable at the West Midlands outfit.

However, with a run of Ipswich, Everton and Crystal Palace to come in England's top flight, Emery will be optimistic that his team can turn around their fortunes.

Furthermore, Villa make the long trip to East Anglia looking to prolong a streak that has lasted more than four decades.

When the teams met in the 2024-25 Premier League campaign, they played out draws at their respective grounds.

Nevertheless, Villa earning a 2-2 draw on their travels extended their unbeaten streak at Portman Road to 10 matches.

Not since September 1984 have they suffered defeat at the home of the Tractor Boys, while Ipswich have incredibly only prevailed twice since that occasion.

#153044. ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now.Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo.
  • According to recent reports, the news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking.
  • AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now.Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo.

According to recent reports, the news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking. For months, reports have mounted of artificial-intelligence models toppling some of the toughest problems in mathematics, plunging the field into turmoil. But the latest claim was the most shocking yet: an AI model had helped to solve the field’s most famous open problem, the Riemann hypothesis.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

Recent findings suggest that the proof was released on 20 November by mathematician Levent Alpöge at AI giant Anthropic in San Francisco, California, who used an advanced version of the firm’s Claude model. It came in the form of 17 million lines of code in the open-source programming language Lean, which translates mathematical arguments into computer-certifiable code. In a matter of hours, a separate set of mathematicians rushed out a human-written proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which is in the branch of number theory and pertains to the randomness of prime numbers.

Alpöge’s proof has been independently verified by the non-profit organization behind Lean and the Mathlib Initiative, which runs the reference library of formalized mathematics results written in Lean. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him,” the community stated in a statement on 21 November.

According to recent reports, the mathematics community has broadly accepted the claim, although responses differ wildly. Some celebrate Alpöge’s achievement, but others see the development as proof that humans are fighting against machines for the future of mathematics.

Nature hears reactions from five mathematicians on what solving the Riemann hypothesis means to them.

Mathematician Tasmin Chu is part of the Association for Human Mathematics, whose members commit to doing AI-free research.Credit: Elizabeth Xiao.

Tasmin Chu, PhD student in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena.

A technology that can autonomously prove the Riemann hypothesis is no trivial matter. I think that it is imperative our society acts to pause AI development as soon as possible. Over the past year, mathematical institutions have faced the impossible task of adapting to the rapidly changing capabilities of AI in real time.

It’s enormously disruptive for early-career researchers — the people who are the intellectual future of our field. Soon other sectors of society will face the same issues.

Sources indicate that my reaction is grave concern. AI companies urgently require democratic oversight. I do not think AI’s encroachment into math is inevitable, nor is the death of human mathematical practice inevitable. It’s a choice to disempower ourselves, just as it’s a choice to continue building these technologies despite grave safety concerns. I continue to practice mathematics without LLMs, because I believe it’s critical that scientific inquiry continues in the hands of human beings. Some of us at the Association for Human Mathematics — whose organizing committee I am on — are collectively making the same decision.

Harini Desiraju, lecturer in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.

Recent findings suggest that given the events of the past few months, this news wasn't entirely a surprise, but we need to wait to understand the Lean proof and let the experts verify it. It is several million lines of code, after all.

I am not a number theorist, so I might not have the same emotional attachment to the Riemann hypothesis. Nevertheless, I have deep appreciation for the ubiquity and the importance of the problem in several areas of maths and physics.

Recent findings suggest that as for the recent events, I want to distinguish between formal proofs versus knowledge. It is an impressive feat to solve such a problem. However, because it is a Lean proof over millions of lines, it is going to take a while before the community gets real understanding, and validity of the proof. With an AI-independent approach available as well, it could present a great opportunity for discovery of newly introduced ideas and mathematics. We need to see how it all plays out.

Sources indicate that there is another discussion to be had, which involves the role of frontier labs in research. Most of us see the potential benefits of this technology, but it is of utmost importance that we work towards a future where the agency is with the scientific community and not a couple of companies.

Mathematician Marcus Du Sautoy is anxious about what’s next for his field.Credit: David Levenson/Getty.

Marcus Du Sautoy, mathematician and professor for the public understanding of science at the University of Oxford, UK.

Industry observers note that it was real mix of emotions. A part of me claims, how exciting to be alive when this great problem was solved! I think even when Fermat’s last theorem was solved, we had the same excitement and the same melancholy: that great motivator is gone.

According to recent reports, mixed in with that, is the complete surprise that it ended up being proved this way. If you’d asked me three months ago, I would never have predicted it.

There’s quite a lot of anxiety about what ‘math 2.0’ is going to look like.

Xin Zhang, assistant professor in mathematics at the University of Hong Kong.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03835-0.

These interviews have been edited for length and clarity.

Oliver Glasner has criticised Nottingham Forest players that cannot speak English after being in the country for several years, as he called for higher standards at the club.

Forest are at the moment outside the Premier League relegation zone on goal difference after 11 matches, having won just twice in the top flight since Glasner's arrival in the summer.

Speaking ahead of their Friday night clash against Chelsea, Glasner highlighted the failure of some of his squad to learn English to illustrate how standards needed to rise at the club.

It has been revealed that 'Stability in a company is having standards,' Glasner mentioned. 'Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough.

'We have players who are here for four years, can't speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language.

'For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English. If I want to manage in Italy, I have to speak Italian.

Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner has criticised stars for failing to speak English years after joining the club.

Glasner highlighted the issue as an example as he insisted standards need to rise at the club.

'Otherwise, Oliver Glasner, if you want to speak in your dialect, stay at home in Austria, everybody understands you, but nowhere else.'.

Football clubs regularly enlist the services of language experts in an effort to help foreign stars to settle and communicate with their team-mates.

West Brom and Wolves have worked with Language Partners for around 20 years, with the tech giant providing tailored classes to players and coaches, offering specific skills required for their role at the clubs.

Another manufacturer, Communicate Well, has worked with Premier League clubs since 1999, with lessons taking place at training grounds, players’ homes and ‘out and about’ to provide real-life tasks in English.

Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez previously revealed Arsenal had included a £20,000 bonus in his first contract with the club, which would be paid when he passed the English proficiency test.

Martinez, who signed for Arsenal in the summer of 2010 from Argentine side Independiente, had reportedly passed the test before Christmas.

English stars moving abroad have received praise in recent years for their efforts to learn the native language, with Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Trent Alexander-Arnold having all made efforts to become fluent in Spanish.

Recent findings suggest that alexander-Arnold revealed he had worked with a Spanish tutor for five months prior to joining Real Madrid. The tutor revealed he had started ‘from zero’ but worked every day to be able to speak Spanish at his unveiling at the club.

After speaking Spanish at his Barcelona unveiling, Gordon explained he had initially begun learning the language at Everton when working under Rafael Benitez. He later spoke Spanish with a physio at Newcastle as he targeted a move to Barcelona, while the winger also underwent six formal lessons.

Joao Gomes is among Wolves' foreign imports to have worked with a specialist language tech giant to help them settle at the club.

Arsenal put a bonus in Emiliano Martinez's contract to encourage him to learn English.

Trent Alexander-Arnold worked with a Spanish tutor for five months before his move to Real Madrid.

Daily Mail Sport reported last month that Glasner had not been happy with some of his players' attitudes and their response to his work since joining the club from Crystal Palace in the summer.

Glasner had explosively hit out at his players after their 2-0 defeat at Brentford at the end of October, with the Austrian having warned players either had to buy into his methods to see a turnaround in form or they would have a sixth manager since the start of last season.

The 52-year-old's warning appeared to have been met with a positive response as Forest earned a stunning 3-1 victory over Man City before the international break, but they returned with a 2-0 loss at Bournemouth last weekend.

Glasner had maintained that his squad will have to work hard and show commitment both on and off the pitch to improve.

'We always try to support the players to get the best version of themselves that they can be. But at the end, the players that have to do it, they have to buy in, they have to listen and work hard on the pitch,' Glasner mentioned.

'There is no other opportunity to improve, it would be easy laying on the sofa and doing nothing and you become a better football player or suddenly speak a language all of a sudden.

According to recent reports, 'It just doesn't work. It is all about how hard you work and how committed you are.

Glasner has insisted his squad need to work hard and show commitment to improve.

'I believe none of our players have reached his personal ceilings so far, there is always bits to improve – physically, mentally, technically, tactically – there is always space to improve.

'The most vital thing is that players want to improve, then it can happen.'.

Glasner met with Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis in London earlier this week, where intends for the January transfer window were discussed.

Forest are expected to target adding around five players to their squad in the window as they bid to turn around their fortunes.

'He was asking "what do you need, what do you want here to improve in the squad, the staff and the environment",' Glasner said.

'He wants the best for Nottingham Forest, he wants the best for everyone here.

Sources indicate that 'We need to improve in the squad, in the staff, in the environment and this is our discussion. It was a fantastic meeting and it was worth spending six hours travelling.'.

Forest face a Chelsea side on Friday that have lost three of their last four league matches.

Glasner’s side will then begin December with matches against Hull, Brighton and Sunderland as they bid to climb the table.

Industry observers note that PEC Zwolle finished just outside the bottom three last season, and their start to the 2026-27 campaign came as little surprise. They collected just four points from their opening eight matches, including a heavy 7-0 defeat to Feyenoord.

Taking over from interim Dennis van der Ree, Alex Pastoor made a winning start to life in the dugout thanks to a 3-1 win over Telstar, thanks to a Dylan Mbayo double and Ibrahim Cissoko’s early second-half strike.

The decision to part ways with Henry van der Vegt in October has since paid off, with Zwolle collecting 11 of a possible 15 points since his departure - the Eredivisie’s third-best return over that period.

Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace firm Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
  • The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
  • "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier noted in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace firm Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier noted in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business.".

According to recent reports, he also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments.".

Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

Industry observers note that she says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors.".

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It states it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, claims the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential concern is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak states it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen.".

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

In a recent development, "The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things.".

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

It has been revealed that "Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously.".

In a recent development, it was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' strategy to develop a upcoming single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce.".

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union.".

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

It has been revealed that "We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development.".

Industry observers note that last weekend, Spurs enjoyed a historic result, beating Chelsea 2-0 at Stamford Bridge for only the second time in the league for 36 years thanks to Mike Penders’ own goal and Mathys Tel’s stunning solo strike. The 1-0 League Cup victory over Fulham in midweek has momentarily eased the pressure on the Frenchman, but given their newfound success in recent campaigns, fan expectations have risen, with recent performances prompting some cause for concern.

Tottenham remain without the suspended Rodrigo Bentancur, while Xavi Simons, Wilson Odobert, Lucas Bergvall, Savio, Tosin Adarabioyo and Mykhaylo Mudryk are out injured. By Ben Sully | 27 Nov 2026 13:13, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 13:52.

Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa has ruled out a January move for Manchester United-linked Calvin Bassey.

Man United right now have the Premier League's second-worst defensive record after shipping 23 goals in 11 games.

As a result, the Red Devils are widely expected to bolster their backline when the transfer window opens for business in the new year.

Bassey is among those who have been mentioned as a potential target, having established himself as an accomplished Premier League centre-back during his time with Fulham.

However, Arbeloa has dampened Man United's hopes of a January swoop, insisting the focus is on agreeing a new contract with Bassey rather than entertaining the prospect of a winter sale.

“I’m so happy with Calvin and obviously he is not on sale," Arbeloa told reporters ahead of Sunday's Premier League clash against Bournemouth.

"No chance he can leave this club in January and I think he is happy here. He is one of our captains, he is one of our leaders.

According to recent reports, "It is normal that so many clubs are interested in him, it is good for him and good for us. It means he is performing really well.

"We are working on a new contract, and I hope he can sign as soon as possible.”.

Bassey's current contract is set to expire at the end of the season, although Fulham hold the option to trigger a 12-month extension.

Speaking about last weekend's draw with Manchester City, Bassey remarked: "We’re still negotiating, we’re still talking and obviously it’s an amazing place to be.

Industry observers note that "I’ve settled in nicely and the manager has put a lot of faith and trust in me. So, it’s nice to be here and hopefully we will see what happens with the negotiations.".

Bassey has started all 11 of Fulham's Premier League games this season and has formed a strong central defensive partnership with summer signing David Affengruber.

The pair have helped Fulham build a five-game unbeaten league run in which they have conceded no more than one goal in any of the five matches.

Juventus captain Manuel Locatelli has called his knee injury one of the hardest spells of his career. Answering questions from young members of the club, he remarked his recovery is on track and that he has learned to live with a long wait.

Manuel Locatelli has not played since early September, and the Juventus captain admits the time away has been tough. Speaking in a fresh episode of the club’s Junior Reporter series, in which children from the Juventus membership programme interview a first team player, the midfielder was open about how he is coping.

As ANSA reported on Tuesday evening, Locatelli put the injury alongside Italy’s failure to reach the World Cup as the lowest points of his time as a professional.

According to recent reports, locatelli explained that he hurt his knee and now has to stay off the pitch for a long time. He remarked he feels good and that the work is going well, much of it in the gym rather than on the grass.

Sources indicate that “I miss playing football so much, so much, but I have learned to accept this situation,” he told the young reporters, according to the quotes carried by Calciomercato.com. He added that he knows he has to give it time, and that he must do his best to come back in good shape.

On the national team, he did not hide the pain of missing out on the tournament. “When you lose, and lose like that, it is a moment of suffering,” he stated.

It has been revealed that the problem dates back to 6 September, when Locatelli sprained his right knee in the 1-1 home draw against Milan. Two days later Juventus confirmed in an official medical upgrade that he had undergone surgery in Lyon to suture the external meniscus. Dr Bertrand Sonnery-Cottet carried out the operation with club doctor Marco Freschi in attendance, and rehabilitation started the following day.

Recent findings suggest that the club gave no return date at the time. ANSA now claims the captain expects to be available again in the first months of 2027, while Football Italia reports that he is not expected back in full training before March.

It has been revealed that locatelli also spoke about leadership. He said becoming captain was an ambition he had from the moment he arrived from Sassuolo in 2021, and he credited Giorgio Chiellini, Leonardo Bonucci and Danilo for showing him what it means to be present for the group every day. His childhood idols, he said, were Pavel Nedved, Gianluigi Buffon, Alessandro Del Piero and Francesco Totti.

The club tied him down in April, when he signed a latest contract until June 2030.

His absence has forced Luciano Spalletti to reshape his midfield for most of the autumn, a problem we looked at when Thuram and Locatelli were both missing earlier this month.

Juventus host Omonia in the Europa League on Thursday on the back of a 4-0 win over Venezia, and go to Como on Sunday with a clean bill on the disciplinary front, as covered in our piece on the matchday 12 rulings. Their captain, for now, remains a spectator, but by his own account a patient one.

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has revealed that captain Bruno Fernandes is a major doubt for Saturday's Premier League clash with Brentford due to an illness.

Fernandes was unable to train on Friday, having picked up a virus.

Pochettino has said that no final decision has been made on the Portugal international at this stage of proceedings, but he is a major doubt for the game with the Bees.

"We will not take any risks. We will see when he wakes up tomorrow," Pochettino told reporters during Friday's press conference at Carrington.

There has been criticism of Fernandes' form this season, but he has still come up with eight goals and three assists in 16 appearances for the Red Devils during the 2026-27 campaign.

The 32-year-old scored twice against his former club Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League on Wednesday night and had been in line to start against Brentford.

Fernandes now has four goals and one assist in five Champions League appearances this season, in addition to four goals and two assists in 10 Premier League matches.

Man United will also again be missing Benjamin Sesko, Carlos Baleba and Marcus Rashford through injury this weekend, but Luke Shaw returned to the bench against Sporting and could potentially receive some minutes in this contest.

The Red Devils will be going in search of just their second Premier League win of the campaign against Brentford.

A disastrous campaign to date has left the Red Devils in 19th spot in the Premier League table, claiming only eight points from their first 11 games of the season.

Industry observers note that "This is a group of players who want to do well, who want to perform. Our job is to build confidence. We arrive full of energy, positive, but it's difficult for the players when the results haven't been up to scratch, but we try to help them as best we can," added Pochettino.

Man United have lost two of their last three Premier League matches against Brentford, but they recorded a 2-1 win over the Bees in the corresponding game earlier this season.
