📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 06:47 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 08:49 EST, 26 November 2026.

The female reporter Jude Bellingham defended during an 'intimidating' post-match interview has praised the England star for being 'respectful' and 'well-mannered' as she opened up on the viral incident.

BBC Sport reporter Elizabeth Conway was speaking to Bellingham after Real Madrid's 5-1 win over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday when another journalist interrupted her as she posed a follow-up question, threatening to cut her interview short.

But the midfielder, 23, refused to answer the interferer and instead told him: 'Sorry, she's got one more [question].'.

Bellingham, who scored a sensational long-range goal on the hour mark to put Real Madrid ahead in the Champions League clash, was widely praised after footage of the incident went viral on social media, with fans applauding him as a 'class act' and 'role model for young men'.

Now Conway has added to the praise, stating the experience 'added a whole fresh layer to the love people have for Jude'.

Conway had been waiting to speak to the England star in the 'mixed zone' after the match – an area where journalists line up behind a barrier to interview players.

Jude Bellingham has won praise for his 'respectful' and 'classy' treatment of a female reporter.

Sources indicate that BBC reporter Elizabeth Conway had been interrupted by a male reporter when asking her second question, leading to Bellingham's intervention. Source: instagram/@elizabeth.conway_.

'It is utter carnage,' she told BBC Radio WM, opening up on the incident at the Bernabeu. 'Obviously as an English reporter at Real Madrid, getting Jude is exactly what we want, it's gold dust.

'Jude very rarely gives interviews, especially in the mixed zone. It is chaos... It's kind of every person out for themselves.

'You've got elbows, you've got microphones, you've got cameras, you've got massive tall men reaching over you.

'I'm one of very, very few female reporters and one of very, very few English reporters there, so trying to make a stand for yourself and get in a good position is so key.'.

Conway admitted the mixed zone can be an 'intimidating' environment and being interrupted is unfortunately a routine part of being a post-match interviewer.

Admitting it was 'so nice' that Bellingham stepped in to stand up for her, she added: 'It's shown him yet again being respectful, polite, and really respecting me as a journalist.'.

Conway, originally from Solihull, specialises in Spanish football and is based in Madrid, according to her Instagram, where she has more than 12,000 followers.

She had asked Bellingham in the mixed zone what had gone through his mind when he scored with his sensational effort at the Bernabeu.

'Yeah, I was a bit surprised honestly,' Bellingham noted. 'I knew I could control the ball and get it into my grasp, but normally from there I am looking to see who's on as an option to play through.

Sources indicate that 'It popped up nicely and I thought, you know, I am just going to hit it. It was a nice goal and important for the team being the second goal and gave us control.'.

The England superstar (right) had been in-demand after scoring with a stunning volley to inspire Real Madrid to beat PSV Eindhoven in the Champions League on Tuesday night.

After being interrupted and encouraged by Bellingham to pose her second question, Conway asked whether he feels like he is in the form of his life for club and country.

'My mentality is based more around just focusing on the next game, I think you are only as good as your next one. Your last one doesn't really matter,' Bellingham added.

'Even this one that has just gone past, it is all well and good and speaking to you guys is fun but my focus has to change now to preparing for the next game.'.

Conway later shared the exchange on social media, writing: 'Just Jude waiting for me to finish my questions,' adding a handshake emoji while fans were quick to praise Bellingham for his 'classy' moment.

Speaking post-match, Bellingham was clear where he ranked his goal, declaring: 'I think this was the best goal of my life.'.

The strike comes a day after Daily Mail Sport reported the 23-year-old is in advanced talks over a new Real Madrid contract that will make him one of the best-paid players in Europe.

Madrid have been eager to tie down the in-form England midfielder beyond his current contract, understood to be worth around £12.5million a year after tax, which runs until 2029, in recognition of his performances.

Bellingham has previously earned plaudits for his treatment of the media, having stopped to speak to a disabled reporter during the World Cup when several of his England team-mates had walked past, taking the time to answer his questions in Spanish.

There is currently a host of speculation surrounding Paz's future with Como.

Paz arrived at Como from Real Madrid in the summer of 2024, and he has represented the Italian team on 91 occasions, scoring 25 goals and registering 25 assists.

Paz has a contract with Como until the summer of 2028, but Real Madrid do have the option to re-sign Paz for £67m next year.

Man United have allegedly activated a further year on captain Bruno Fernandes' contract to take him to the summer of 2028, but there is still uncertainty surrounding the Portugal international's future.

According to The Athletic, the 20-time English champions view Paz as a potential replacement for Fernandes, should the experienced attacker leave Old Trafford.

Journalist David Ornstein claims that Paz is not presently looking to return to Real Madrid, allegedly as he is unsure how much football he would receive due to the presence of Jude Bellingham in the number 10 position at Bernabeu.

Man United are said to appeal to Paz, even considering their current struggles, with the Red Devils expected to be in the race for the Argentina international in 2027.

Paz shares an agent with new Man United head coach Mauricio Pochettino, which has also allegedly strengthened the English club's hand when it comes to a potential race.

The attacker is a 16-time Argentina international, scoring six goals and registering two assists for his country, and is currently viewed as one of the best playmakers in world football.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

José Mourinho had a lot to say after Real Madrid’s stunning victory over Celta Vigo. Jostled by the Galicians, the Merengues had to fight to snatch a precious success thanks to Bellingham and Carlos Espi. A more complicated meeting than expected for the Portuguese technician, who notably pointed out the fatigue of his internationals and the lack of concentration of his team at the start of the match. But at the press conference, the Special One especially put on a show when discussing his offensive choices. Asked about Carlos Espí, who continues to be decisive despite limited playing time, Mourinho explained at length the qualities of his striker. “He’s a surface player. When you dominate an opponent who is content to defend, his game is devastating. He has quality in the area, he plays with his back to goal, he is good with his head, he attacks both posts… He has all the qualities of an area player. History is full of players like him, decisive even with limited playing time”he noted.

Sources indicate that and Mourinho was keen to underline the impeccable state of mind of his player, who does not seem disturbed by his status in the Madrid offensive hierarchy. “We are happy with him. He’s the kind of player who doesn’t get distracted by discussions about his playing time: Should Kylian be a substitute or play more? He knows that he is progressing, that he has the respect of the coach, his teammates and the supporters. He is happy. And I hope to have the opportunity to give him tenure, 90 minutes or more”continued the Portuguese. A way of also justifying the use and playing time of Carlos Espi with a Madrid team rather focused on offensive transitions and depth.

It has been revealed that but the José Mourinho show really began when a journalist asked him if he was considering combining Kylian Mbappé and Carlos Espí at the forefront of his attack. A possibility that Mourinho does not completely rule out, but which would pose serious balance problems for his team. And the Portuguese technician found a rather original way of explaining it. “I can do it, but when we lose the ball, I, being on the sideline, will have to enter the field in transition and punch someone to stop the counter-attack! Because playing with two pure strikers means the wingers have to defend inside. And it will certainly not be Diomandé, Vinicius, Arda… A little Brahim, perhaps. But with the characteristics of our wingers, we are not made to play in a classic 4-4-2”he said. Behind the joke, Mourinho insisted on the tactical constraints of such an association. “It’s more complicated than you might think. It’s easier for the supporters, as well as for you. But the reality is a little more difficult. ».

It has been revealed that finally, José Mourinho also took advantage of this press conference to end the suspense concerning Vinicius Junior. While questions surrounded the presence of the Brazilian in the starting lineup during the next meeting in Madrid with his goals for Brazil during the break, the Special One preferred to cut short speculation with his usual humor. “I said it yesterday, it doesn’t matter whether he’s a substitute or a starter. To avoid you asking me the question on Monday and having too much to say, I’m going to be a bad boy and end the story: he will start Tuesday in the Champions League.he confirmed. An answer which has the merit of being clear, while Mourinho wants to juggle and alternate between offensive positions. And after a difficult victory against Celta Vigo, the Madrid coach recalled that at Real Madrid, aligning all the offensive talents was not necessarily enough to build a balanced team.

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

Sources indicate that A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

It has been revealed that few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta mentioned, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

According to recent reports, “There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

Industry observers note that the result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

Sources indicate that A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

In a recent development, “That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

Celebrating Neil Warnock & his most infamous dressing room meltdown

💡 Key Takeaways
  • “The public perception of Neil Warnock is definitely different to the reality of what the guy is.”.
  • So says Shaun Derry, who played under Warnock at Crystal Palace and QPR and must know a thing or two about what makes the infamously irate manager tick.
  • It has been revealed that the theme of split personalities crops up time and again when former players discuss their time with him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The public perception of Neil Warnock is definitely different to the reality of what the guy is.”.

So says Shaun Derry, who played under Warnock at Crystal Palace and QPR and must know a thing or two about what makes the infamously irate manager tick.

It has been revealed that the theme of split personalities crops up time and again when former players discuss their time with him. Away from football, Colin Neil is portrayed as a laid-back guy, enjoying the company of his family down in Cornwall.

Warnock himself gifted us with this beautifully idyllic image: “I cut the grass and feed the ducks and listen to the birds singing,” he told Cornwall Live about his life during lockdown.

But simply watching Warnock during a football match is enough to raise your blood pressure.

The veteran manager, arguably the most Yorkshire male in existence, doesn’t burden his players with complex tactical instructions. But he does expect his players to follow those instructions down to the last fuckin’ letter.

It’s at this point we should introduce Chris Morgan. A famously combative centre-back, Morgan was sent off six times for both Barnsley and Sheffield United, holding the record for red cards at both clubs.

If ever a player represented a manager on the pitch, it was Morgan under Warnock at Bramall Lane. And, to paraphrase Eminem, when a tornado meets a volcano you get explosive results. Explosive and hilarious results.

Industry observers note that years before Amazon premiered their ‘All or Nothing’ series, Warnock allowed the cameras to document Sheffield United’s 2004-05 season. We can only hope it was him that insisted on the final title – ‘Warnock’.

What must have seemed like a good idea at the time began to look ill-judged as the club’s push for the Premier League started to falter.

And the most iconic moment of a must-watch film came after a home match against Wolves in 2004.

Gotta laugh at archive Neil Warnock going at Chris Morgan back in the day! 😂.

🎥 Sky Sports pic.twitter.com/y8mB4OJlxb.

— Empire of the Kop (@empireofthekop) June 21, 2017.

It has been revealed that leading 3-2 against the pre-season promotion favourites, United conspired to allow Joleon Lescott to plunder a late equaliser. Not only had two points been dropped, but the mother of all fuses had been lit.

As the dejected Blades players re-entered the dressing room, Warnock stood waiting with hands on his hips and ready to ask the burning question: “Who’s got him?”.

Phil Jagielka, wearing what appears to be a Selkirk Rex on his head, began to protest his innocence before Morgan took over.

Recent findings suggest that “Olofinjana, fuckin’ Cort,” the captain said while extending a finger to denote each player. This explanation held no dice with Warnock, who retorted: “Who do you have to pick up, eh? Is it f*ckin’ black and white?”.

Upon hearing the word “Lescott”, which Morgan reluctantly spat out like a teenager being caught by their parents smuggling alcohol in a water bottle, Warnock threw his hands in dismay.

In a recent development, “In the last f*ckin’ two minutes,” he cried, “can’t ya f*ckin’ get him in the time it comes to take a f*ckin’ kick? Can ya not get to pick him up by the time it comes from there to there? Whoever’s in the f*ckin’ box?”.

William Shakespeare and Charles Dickens have contributed much to the English language, but neither were a patch on Warnock at expressing the frustration at conceding to a late set-piece.

Rather than admit defeat, Morgan doubled down: “There’s f*ckin’ three massive ones at the back. Craddock and the two other f*ckin’ big f*ckers. So what do we do?”.

In a recent development, it’s at this point that Warnock’s simmering kettle boiled over. “YOU PICK LESCOTT. IF ONE OF THE OTHERS SCORE, I DON’T F*CKIN’ BLAME YOU. YOU PICK YOUR F*CKIN’ MAN UP. IF HE’S THE SPARE MAN, I TAKE THE F*CKIN’ BLAME.”.

Industry observers note that to his credit, Morgan continued to stand his ground. As Warnock trudged towards the camera, the centre-back stated: “It isn’t f*ckin’ black and white gaffer,” as if appealing to his manager’s logic represented the best form of defence. “You pick up whoever’s f*ckin’ there.”.

Morgan was a man clearly prepared to die on the hill of zonal marking, but Warnock failed to accept the contrasting point of view.

“So Lescott’s got nobody on him, has he?” he replied, with all the comprehension of a pensioner using an iPad for the first time.

Now it was Morgan’s turn to flip. As Jagielka tried to atone for his sins in the background, his defensive partner grabbed the nearest bottle of Powerade and introduced it across the dressing room.

“I’ll pick up f*ckin’ four of ’em then,” he shouted, exhibiting all the defensiveness Warnock wished he’d shown on the pitch.

Sheffield United failed to gain promotion that season but, with Warnock and Morgan leading from the front, they reached the Premier League the following campaign.

Recent findings suggest that morgan speaks warmly of his former manager. After Warnock guided Cardiff to the top flight in 2018, he told the BBC: “He’ll be honest with you and people have all seen the videos in the dressing room, but Monday morning it’s all forgotten about and he’s back to his jokey self.”.

After going toe-to-toe with his boss, with side-splitting results, Morgan knows that better than most.

Latest Update: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
  • This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.
  • According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

In a recent development, his two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible.".

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers.".

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he remarked.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach.".

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

According to recent reports, "In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides.".

Industry observers note that for several weeks already, his fate had been sealed. Michael Carrick was finally dismissed from his position this Thursday, after meeting his now ex-leaders the same morning. Omar Berrada, the general manager, and Jason Wilcox, the football director, informed him of the end of the adventure, three days after the announcement of his imminent departure. It is this method that is being singled out today by the press and observers, more than the dismissal of the Manchester United coach. The situation was becoming inevitable.

It has been revealed that while he knew he was doomed since Monday morning, the day after the draw at Old Trafford against Aston Villa (4-4), the technician continued his mission, biding his time. His representatives had been contacted by management to announce their intentions to separate. Except that in the meantime, Berrada and Wilcox hopped on a plane to Monaco to meet the club’s co-owner, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, and finalize the details together. Only returning to Manchester on Wednesday evening, they then called Carrick to arrange a meeting the following morning.

According to The Telegraphthis way of doing things and this very long wait upset the former midfielder. He did not understand why he had to organize the sessions on Tuesday and Wednesday, without most of the management players, who had left for selection, but with his assistants: Steve Holland, Jonathan Woodgate, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, all fired since yesterday. At the same time, MU was working on the arrival of Mauricio Pochettino. In this tense context, made of mutual reproaches and delaying tactics, the information inevitably leaked.

In a recent development, “Over the past 24 to 48 hours, the situation has been catastrophic. While the manager, a club legend, directs training on the field, the management and owner are in Monaco, and simultaneously contact the American Football Federation to approach Mauricio Pochettino», jumps Gary Neville in the still very popular podcast, Stick to Football by The Overlap. “It’s simply sickening. This is well below the standards expected in any other organization, in any other industry. This would be unfair dismissal and you would be prosecuted», Continues the former Mancunian defender.

“Being in Monaco while the team, the staff and the people who manage the club on a daily basis are in Manchester is very frowned upon, and it casts a negative light on the management. I don’t think anyone will come out of this unscathed.» Strong words which echo those made the day before by Peter Schmeichel, another legend of the Red Devils of the 90s. «If they look for someone else, let them relieve him of his duties! Don’t let him come and lead the training. He did it again yesterday (Wednesday). How disrespectful is that?», asked the former goalkeeper.

In a recent development, faced with Carrick’s anger, management tried to defend itself, again according to The Telegraph. She understands the frustration of the 45-year-old technician and regrets that their separation happened like this. She also denies having carried out all the checks (notably legal) prior to and necessary for dismissal, before communicating her decision to the person concerned. The club believes it has demonstrated all possible transparency. These explanations will not convince many people as Manchester United is used to these procedures. The dismissal of Amorim, for example, is less than a year old….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 08:48 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 10:35 EST, 26 November 2026.

A referee was replaced at half-time of an Asian Football Confederation (AFC) Champions League Two match after he was accused of 'being drunk' by a manager of one of the teams – a claim the official has denied.

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab oversaw the match between United Arab Emirates' side Al Jazira and Iran's Gol Gohar in Asia's second tier club competition.

Controversy emerged in the 32nd minute after Hattab awarded a free-kick after a foul by Al Jazira's Felício Milson.

Hattab initially waved away protests from Al-Jazira players and approached Milson holding a yellow card.

The official then stunned players after appearing to receive a message in his earpiece, before turning and walking towards Al-Jazira goalkeeper Ersin Destanoglu.

Hattab indicated the goalkeeper a yellow card, despite him being nearly half the pitch away from the incident.

Referee Hanna Hattab was accused by a manager of 'being drunk' following a controversial decision in an Asian Champions League Two match - a claim the official has denied.

The referee was then seen speaking to his fourth official, leading to him rescinding the goalkeeper's yellow card while Milson escaped being shown a second yellow card for his challenge.

Al Jazira scored the only goal of the game minutes later through Anderson Talisca, but the bizarre incident involving Hattab was reportedly the centre of discussion at half-time.

Gol Gohar head coach Mehdi Rahmati had reportedly been seen shouting 'he's drunk' at the official, while the club's sporting director claimed post-match they would have refused to play the second half had Hattab remained in charge.

'The referee against Al Jazira was not in a normal state, and even Al Jazira's players told us the same thing,' said Heydar Afsari.

'The club immediately informed the match officials and warned them that we would not play if the situation remained the same.'.

Hattab was ultimately replaced by the fourth official for the second half of the match.

The referee, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing pool, has since released a statement hitting back at the allegation.

'I will wait for the official communication and official stance from the Syrian Arab Football Federation, and I will also communicate with the people and parties responsible for me locally and internationally, before issuing an official statement that clarifies all the details and facts related to what happened,' Hattab wrote.

The claim had centred on the referee appearing to listen to his earpiece and changing his mind on booking an Al Jazira player, before bizarrely showing a yellow card to their goalkeeper.

Al Jazira's goalkeeper appeared stunned by his yellow card, which was later rescinded with the referee then being replaced at half-time of the match.

'In conclusion, I confirm that family and personal life are not the responsibility of others, and are not a game in your hands.

'Religion, reason, and morals do not tolerate the insult of people's privacy or defamation of them.

'I also confirm my full right to take all legal and judicial measures against anyone who published or made a statement or contributed to the insult and defamation of me, regardless of their position or status, whether they are an individual, an institution, or a sports entity.'.

Omani sports journalist Issa Noted, who covers Asian competitions, also came to Hattab's defence and insisted the claim the official was drunk is false.

'What happened to him was due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus,' he wrote on social media,.

'He underwent a medical examination after the match and was not intoxicated, contrary to what has been circulating.'.

The Syrian Football Federation added in a statement: 'Following an assessment of his health, it has been confirmed - contrary to various claims circulating on social media- that the reports regarding his situation are entirely unfounded.

'The Committee reiterates its unwavering support for him and is committed to thoroughly investigating all details and circumstances surrounding the incident.

'In this regard, the Committee has contacted the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) to request the referee’s medical report, the match commissioner’s report, and the referee assessor’s report, in order to accurately ascertain the facts of the incident and take the necessary follow-up actions.'.

Roberto Mancini wasn’t at Leicester long, but he left an indelible mark

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Planetfootball

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Roberto Mancini only played five games in a Leicester City shirt, but the former Italy international certainly left his mark.
  • Industry observers note that looking at the Foxes’ signings during the 2000-01 season, there are a few names who you might not remember too fondly.
  • Junior Lewis played 25 league games for Leicester.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roberto Mancini only played five games in a Leicester City shirt, but the former Italy international certainly left his mark.

Industry observers note that looking at the Foxes’ signings during the 2000-01 season, there are a few names who you might not remember too fondly. Or, indeed, at all.

Junior Lewis played 25 league games for Leicester. Simon Royce made it to 19. Kevin Ellison managed just one. However, as Mancini proved, minutes on the pitch aren’t the only thing that can help you make an impact.

After playing his part in Lazio’s run to the Serie A title in 1999-2000, his third season in Rome, the Italian forward was sidelined the following year.

Indeed, as we entered 2001, he had gone more than six months without so much as stepping onto the pitch at the Stadio Olimpico, with his player-coach role under Sven-Goran Eriksson turning into a coaching job alone.

Enter Leicester, who went into the fresh year with three straight defeats – including a 6-1 drubbing at Arsenal – and found themselves in need of refreshment.

“Roberto knows that he is 36 and that I am looking for his football knowledge, not his legs,” admitted manager Peter Taylor in a display of honesty which we don’t often see these days.

“He also understands that his role will be to help bring on the younger players and pass on experience to the strikers.”.

In a recent development, those strikers, summer arrivals Ade Akinbiyi and Trevor Benjamin, took some of the blame for the lack of goals which brought about Leicester’s relegation the following season. If Mancini had stayed longer, perhaps things could have gone differently.

DID YOU KNOW? #BPL winning manager Roberto Mancini made 4 appearances for Leicester City in 2001 #BPLkickoff pic.twitter.com/6rBNVaTtz5.

— Premier League (@premierleague) July 22, 2014.

He may have been getting on in years, but Mancini still oozed class, something he revealed during the twilight of his career at Lazio.

He was the sort of player who you just knew could score the simple goal if he wanted to, but often felt compelled to remind you he was better than you by doing something more extravagant.

And, most importantly, he was the sort of man who could pull off an oversized shirt without it making him look dishevelled.

In a recent development, “I did not have a clue at that stage that he would go on to manage in Italy and win the things he has as a manager. But what I did notice was that he knew about training and he revealed an interest in the way we trained at Leicester,” Taylor would later recall.

This was not a player looking for a final payday, but rather someone who knew his time in the game was finite and wanted to gain a new experience while he still could.

Mancini seemed to know the limits of what he could provide in the other direction but knew he could provide something, and as long as both sides recognised this to begin with it would be enough.

“For a time Mancini looked like a bottle of Frascati which had found itself in the manufacturer of brown ales,” The Guardian‘s David Lacey wrote of one of Mancini’s starts, in a surprise victory over Chelsea, pointing out the contrast between the Italian’s style and the less sophisticated approach taken by his team-mates against higher-ranked opponents.

The Premier League he entered was a far cry from the one in which he would later manage, but at the same time it felt different from the Serie A of his 20s.

In a recent development, english football was in a transition period, with relics of the pre-1992 era being pushed aside to make way for a glossier new millennium. Things were changing in Italy too, but not as drastically.

In a recent development, there was more energy on the pitch, but the style we associated with the competition in the early days of Football Italia remained. It was a kind of beauty with acknowledged flaws, designed to incorporate history rather than moving on from it.

According to recent reports, in making the switch to England when he did, Mancini could bring over some of that mystique without needing to stick around for the teething problems to show themselves. He could leave a bigger mark in five games, therefore, than he might have done in 50.

Industry observers note that mancini’s departure was so sudden that there was little time to react. He departed days before Leicester’s FA Cup meeting with Bristol City, a game in which he was expected to play, after being offered the Fiorentina manager’s job.

“I can’t praise Roberto enough for what he did while he was with us,” Taylor said, and there seemed to be some recognition that part of his impact came from the way he taught those at the club some lessons they could use to help themselves.

Industry observers note that “I was used to watching him on Italian football on TV. To just get changed in the same dressing room as him was an unbelievable feeling and an honour,” Robbie Savage would later say.

The Italian was Mr Bergstrom handing Lisa Simpson his parting note, reminding his peers that everything they learned from him was something they already had hiding within themselves.

We shouldn’t have been surprised when his return to England saw him lead Manchester City to a monumental title. He’d begun working on it more than a decade earlier.

The UEFA executive committee must meet to examine this possibility and seek the approval of the 55 member federations. The choice of a French leader would mark a change in strategy for Europe, which initially hoped to rely on a personality with greater international notoriety, from the field or the sidelines. Philippe Diallo, however, presents the profile of an experienced administrator and has gradually established himself as one of the most assertive opponents of Infantino. Last September, he considered that the initiatives of the FIFA president during and after the 2026 World Cup had seriously damaged the image and unity of football, considering that trust was broken.

It now remains to be seen whether this candidacy can really shake up Gianni Infantino who maintains a very favorable position. Philippe Diallo could count on the support of the vast majority of European associations, but also try to convince several French-speaking federations of the African Football Confederation. A job of persuasion which promises to be particularly complicated, since the outgoing president benefits from numerous relays on the African continent and in other confederations. According to RMC SportInfantino would already have 80 to 90 votes acquired from the votes expected in March 2027. Philippe Diallo’s lack of international notoriety also constitutes a serious handicap, despite his weight within French and European football. THE Guardian also underlines that the multiplication of opposing candidates could ultimately serve the interests of the outgoing president, who would have an easy time presenting himself as the candidate of unity in the face of a divided opposition. The possible appointment of the boss of the FFF would open a new chapter in this political battle, without guaranteeing UEFA the ability to shake Gianni Infantino.

In the final episode of a six-part podcast series about failure in science, Stirling, an emeritus professor at the University of Sussex in Brighton, UK, draws on examples from climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic, environmental campaigns and energy policy.

According to recent reports, so doubling down on that is exactly...it’s like throwing kerosene on the fire. It’s just not going to work to. Your self behaving in this authoritarian way and expect other authoritarianisms to go away.

Sources indicate that we should be informing democracy and achieving these changes through democratic struggle. And science is absolutely essential to that, but only if it conducts itself in an honest way.

One thing that got me going with all this was in back in the ’90 s I was looking at risk assessments, cost-benefit analysis, life cycle assessments.

All these highly technical quantitative assessments in the energy sector.

Cutting a long story short, they were, the energy sector was the place where these things were developed to their most mature, sophisticated form. And if you looked at any given study, you got this really confident idea.

This is what the risks of nuclear are compared to renewables, compared to gas, or whatever it is.

The same with the other methods I mentioned.

And then every single time you stand back and you look at the literature as a whole, not just peer-reviewed literature, but the literature embodied in law.

So the most kind of authoritatively treated source of data on these things, and you found you could get any answer you like across that peer-reviewed literature.

It depends on the framing. The models give you an answer that depends on how you frame the question.

And that for me kind of radicalized me because I realized that none of the committees, none of the reports around the world were fully representing what the literature they were consulting told us, that you can get all kinds of different answers.

And what matters is not just the one answer, the risk, the cost, environmental costs, the ecosystem service.

What matters is how that changes depending on assumptions, that’s how science should speak to policy, but also to society, telling us how these things depend.

The reason I mentioned that, a lot of people talk about lamenting the fact we have policy-based evidence rather than evidence-based policy, and it’s a good point.

You know, you get all kinds of practices making things up all the time, all over the place in every sector.

But my point wasn’t to lambast that. It wasn’t to say, to lament yet again "you guys are just stitching it up." It was to say "Actually, I’ve never yet seen an area where the evidence compels a single policy.".

In a recent development, so even when you do get the best quality evidence, it is never without uncertainties. It’s never without differences of implication for action, depending on which discipline was actually most influential, how the questions were asked, what the baselines were, etc. etc.

So I have yet to see any body of analysis based on evidence that compels a single decision.

So when you hear people talking about evidence-based policy as if there were only one policy that could have been based on the evidence, they’re basically again being post-truth.

They’re (to be a bit more colourful about it, they’re telling porkies.".

Industry observers note that because there will always be values, interests, assumptions at work, and it’s not a bad thing. It’s inevitable.

That’s how science, you know, depends. For instance, on BSE whether vets or were the epidemiologists in charge? He got a very different answer.

And in COVID, you know, again, we-I mean, it’s still too early to say, as Mao stated, I think about the French Revolution, was it? But it’s too early to say.

But you can still see that what was the best way to act on the available evidence, economic as well as epidemiological, and the different ways of interpreting the epidemiological evidence.

It’s very clear now that it’s not so clear-cut what a particular country should do.

Recent findings suggest that different countries do different things. There are different ways of looking back on it, looking at the time and seeing what was good and what was bad.

So, without taking position on either side, it’s far from clear that there was a single definitive action that should have been taken.

In a recent development, I defy anyone to actually come back and defend that. There’ll be a matter of judgment as between really quite radically different policies.

Industry observers note that so COVID is an example of this. I think we had to pretend there was one policy because it was so stressful.

Politicians had to pretend because otherwise they would have to hide behind their chief scientists, literally sometimes, literally behind them on the podium, hiding behind them because they needed that authority to protect them from the inevitable uncertainties that everyone believed were really there, even though they weren’t acknowledging it in the graphs.

I mean, blame management, trust, public acceptance.

These things are the most important commodities in politics. So yeah, and it’s you know apocryphally, people have all kinds of anecdotes out on these advisory committees.

According to recent reports, I’ve served a little bit on some of them. You know, the number of times in which the politicians will intimate, "I won’t hesitate to hide behind you," almost as a joke.

In a recent development, but so you know, scientists respond to that in different ways. But by and large, they think, "Well, okay, we’ve got to be responsible. Let’s give these guys a single prescriptive answer, even though we know among ourselves that we could have got a different answer, but we’ve got a responsibility not to do an to do to do an elevator pitch.".

You know, not to give on the one hand, on the other, as Margaret Thatcher said, "Save me from the two-handed economist. I want a one-handed economist.".

It has been revealed that she wants it because of justification, but actually, it’s a responsibility of the economist, or in this case, a scientist, to actually explain how it does depend. It always does depend.

If they don’t explain that, then they are failing, I would say science, and failing society, failing democracy.

According to recent reports, other things are really complicated. there’s a lot of real challenges. I don’t want to pretend it’s easier than it really is.

It has been revealed that but actually, we shouldn’t be paralyzed by this. Look at science itself. When it developed in the 17th century, motto of the Royal Society, nullius in verba, that was basically saying that principles of accountability, of argument, of deliberation really mattered, of treating people more equally than many institutions do. That’s not the opposite of democracy. That is democracy.

Science was about, in many ways, democratizing knowledge.

Sources indicate that you know, you needed to argue, you need to show evidence and do analyzes in rigorous ways. But it should be open to anyone to do that, and to any perspective, no matter how ridiculous it sounds, if it can substantiate itself.

So science and democracy are not on opposite sides.

So I think, rather than counterpointing them, like science is against democracy, we can’t trust democracy, going to undermine science, actually, see it the other way round: that science is an embodiment of democracy.

It’s when it is at its best. It’s when it’s being democratic about the ability to challenge power inside science, and that’s how we solve the problems of science.

It’s also how we solve the problems at the moment of democracy, which science is, sadly, because it’s forced to be more authoritarian in pretending a singular truth.

It’s forced into that not by democracy, but by power that is also eroding democracy.

So I think the answer is democracy.

Science, when it comes to advise policymakers, yes, please do your best, but don’t think of yourself just giving a single expedient answer so that a politician goes away happy and can act without worrying about blame.

Inform society at large about the assumptions that went into that.

Show how it depends, and if you do that, you’re informing democracy as much as the powerful actors who are, you know, maybe conferring the patronage on the scientists.

Science fails when it’s not being plural enough.

It needs to be plural about who’s involved, about the questions that are asked, about the disciplines that get around the table, about how it conveys its interpretations of its understandings out to society, and it needs to just not be scared of representing that plurality because with that comes the conditions.

It’s not just anything goes. It’s not plural for plurality’s sake.

It’s then saying under what conditions you get answer X or answer Y, and that’s more scientific.

It’s more rigorous to behave in that way.

When science does that, it’s being more scientific when it’s plural. So I think science fails most when it reduces all those kinds of plurality.

To just a singular idea of truth.
